subsubtopic: PRESENTATION OF FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present in both official languages the first report of the Standing Committee on Secretary of State.
This report is the culmination of seven months of work from coast to coast in reviewing the funding criteria of the Women's Program of the Department of Secretary of State. I would like to make some brief points.
The report crosses Party lines and represents all regions and linguistic groups in Canada. This can be considered an overwhelming endorsation by a majority of members of all Parties in the House in terms of strengthening our recommendations to the Government.
Fairness in Funding is anchored on the principles of equality and democracy. As in the Meech Lake Accord and the Venice Summit, nobody got everything they wanted but everybody got something.
We could not have arrived at such a consensus without the invaluable and oft-times moving testimony by many hundreds of witnesses from all 10 provinces and two Territories. The thrill the committee experienced travelling across this great country was intensified by the knowledge that many women travelled unbelievable distances to make their views known in whatever region we touched down. I know that I speak for all committee members when I say, "We thank you. We heard you, and we hope that you will feel that this report made your efforts worthwhile."
Finally, I would like to pay tribute to colleagues on all sides of the House who contributed mightily to our Fairness in Funding report. To my government colleagues, my namesake, the Hon. Member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott), my friend the mediator, the Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Pietz)-

the Hon. Member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Joncas) as well as the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez)-

-and also for the vigorous participation by our alternate but always present Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson); to our colleagues from the Official Opposition, the distinguished Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) and the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin). The committee also expresses thanks for the very constructive co-operation of the two New Democratic Party members who bracket this national report at the western end of the country, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) and the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett). To them I also say "Thank you".
I hope that the Government will seriously consider the recommendations in the report which create objectives and criteria which will work toward the full participation of women in the Canada of the 1990s and beyond into the 21st century.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO USE OF CHEMICAL PESTICIDES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure and honour to present a petition, pursuant to Standing Order 106, the petition being signed by residents of Hinton, Jasper, and Edmonton, Alberta; Ottawa-Hull, Quebec City, Montreal, South Slocan, Slocan Park, New Denver, Winlaw, Kaslow, Nelson, Argenta, Johnson's Landing, and Gray Creek.
The petitioners are concerned about the increasing number of chemicals used as herbicides and insecticides, chemicals that are proven to have harmful effects on human health. In addition, the petitioners believe that these chemicals also produce short and long-term harmful effects on non-target organisms, soil and water.
These chemicals have in past years been registered and approved as safe for their various uses, and the petitioners believe that new chemicals are constantly approved under the same guidelines as the now-proven harmful ones were.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the petitioners ask the House of Commons to initiate a full public inquiry into the safety, testing, registration, regulation and the use of pesticides and the examination of alternate ways of controlling pests, such as biological controls and plant-derived pesticides.

subtopic: PETITIONS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES TO ROAD SAFETY REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present to the House a petition signed by residents of the Province of Prince Edward Island. These petitioners call upon Parliament to amend the existing Canadian safety standard for rear seat-belts in passenger cars.
The petitioners believe that rear seat-belts in passenger cars are inadequate and that the suffering of crash victims could be reduced or avoided through improved seat-belts. They also believe that the cost of medical care for car-crash victims can be reduced or eliminated with improved rear seat-belts.
For these reasons, the petitioners urge Parliament to institute mandatory installation of three-point adjustable lap/shoulder seat-belts for rear-seat passengers. As well, the petitioners request the mandatory installation of front seat airbags.

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, June 4, consideration of Bill C-18, an Act respecting national transportation, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Motion No. 21 A.
That Bill C-18, be amended in Clause 41 by striking out lines 16 to 21 at page 17 and substituting the following therefor:

June 16, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
"rehear any application before deciding it."
He said: Madam Speaker, Motion No. 21 A, as well as Motions Nos. 54A and 52A, are what we call the Fred Turner amendments. Motion No. 21A deletes language which allows the new National Transportation Agency to review decisions only if there has been a change in the facts. Our amendment removes that restriction.
In fact, Bill C-18 is worse than the existing review procedure which allows the CTC to review its own decisions without a change in facts. Many have been critical of the present procedure because any review that the CTC undertakes is a review of its own work.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary is paying close attention because the proper method, especially on matters of enforcement, would be to have the matter forwarded to the independent aviation tribunal which presently reviews Transport Canada air regulations. I say to my hon. friend opposite that there is no way the Fred Turner case could have happened if this procedure had been followed.
In the absence of any interest on the part of the Government to change the presently unfair system, at least this amendment would prevent even more barriers being put in the way of an agency evaluating a decision. Mr. Turner, a fully licensed operator, lost his licence for being late in filing statistical reports. His licence was cancelled and the next day the bank seized his five aircraft, his hangar and equipment.
This morning I received from the Canadian Aviation Safety Board a case of an operator from Schefferville who was involved in the death of eight people. He was operating without a valid operating authority and is still licensed to fly. He was not late filing his reports, but eight people died.
There is a double standard when one loses one's licence for late filing of statistical reports, but only fined when operating without a valid operating authority or safety licence from the Canadian Aviation Safety Board.
Let me give another example. Spur Aviation was operating without a valid operating certificate and was fined $19,500. Mr. Turner appeared as a witness for the Government. However, Spur did not lose anything else and still has its aircraft. There must be a review of such situations.
Motions Nos. 52A and 54A, which we will be debated later, apply to this kind of situation as well. We must bring equity into the entire licensing process.
Mr. Turner lost his licence because he did not file statistical information on time. On the day that he appeared as a witness for the Government, his licence was cancelled. The airline that was being charged, and at which Mr. Turner appeared as a witness for the Government, is still operating without a valid operating authority. I invite the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) to consider the fact that it is flying without a safety certificate from Transport Canada.
We are told by the Government that there will be no compromise on safety, yet is it revoking the licence of that company? No. I suppose the Government will allow it to continue flying until it commits the great offence of not filing statistical information on time.
On September 30, a Beechcraft carrying seven passengers and a pilot crashed near Schefferville, killing all onboard. There was no operating authority, but did the Government pull the licence? Why should it when the operator was up to date in filing statistical information? That is the safety standard about which the Government says there will be no compromise. It is more concerned about the amount of fuel burned and the number of passengers than with how many were killed. The Government must get its priorities straight on aviation licensing.
These amendments are permissive because they state "may" rather than "shall", in allowing agencies to establish regulations regarding an appeal process. Hopefully, a Fred Turner case or one like it will have an element of natural justice because the person who made the original judgment cannot judge the appeal.
I believe that our amendment would guarantee that another case such as Mr. Turner's would be impossible. It allows offences such as failure to file paperwork to be dealt with under the Aeronautics Act, and would provide for fines or suspensions rather than cancellations.
According to Transport Canada regulations, licence cancellations are only issued for the most serious of offences. The reason Turnair's operating authority was cancelled was not because the punishment fitted the crime but because, as an agency, the CTC was not given the authority to fine.
Clause 107 gives that authority. Our amendment to Clause 107 guarantees that these specific clerical contraventions will be punished by a fine not to exceed $1,000. That will better enforce the current regulations on filing documents because the penalty is believable as well as enforceable. Smaller airlines will want to avoid these Fines and large airlines will not feel exempt from them due to their size. Would any CTC bureaucrat cancel Air Canada's licence for not forwarding a form, without first picking up the phone? I doubt it.
It is also more meaningful because some airlines have chosen to operate without an operating authority. Mr. Turner had a valid operating authority, but could not operate because his planes were seized. This latest incident, the documents about which I received this morning, I believe proves the case for these amendments, beginning with Motion 21A. I hope the Government will agree that such a procedure should be available.
The appeal should not come before a tribunal which judged the case in the first place. It should be before another body so that the operator will have a chance, especially when the issue has to do with something so flimsy as the late filing of
June 16, 1987

statistical reports, when those who have accidents which kill people, and without an operating authority, are still operating.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to speak in favour of Motion No. 21A as well. Section 41 limits review of agency decisions or orders to situations where there have been changes in facts and would in practice, I submit, result in virtually no opportunity for review. Instead the NT A would merely be modifying its decisions or orders in light of these changed facts. When the review process circumvents any critical inspection of the agency's conduct, Madam Speaker, where does this leave the individual-and it could be you, me or any Canadian, subject to NTA regulations?
The section as is would mean no review of the agency's exercise of discretion, no review of the procedure followed in making a decision and no review of possible errors in fact or law. The end result is that an individual adversely affected by NTA regulation would have no administrative avenue for review or appeal save for the very expensive and slow route of the Federal Court system. How can we expect small businessmen or businesswomen, subject to these regulations, to challenge the agency in federal court? Is justice only to be available to those Canadians with sufficient funds to obtain it, those with very deep pockets?
The case of Fred Turner, to which the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) referred a moment ago, and his now defunct company Turnair, exemplifies the nightmarish predicament in which an individual may find himself or herself due to the lack of availability of review. In April, 1984, Mr. Turner's air carrier licence was cancelled by the soon to expire Canadian Transport Commission for failure to supply the agency with data of a purely statistical nature. A review of that cancellation order was warranted because many air carriers fail to file such data on time yet continue to hold licences. Is that equal justice for all? There are even licensed carriers with safety violations known by the CTC who have not been subjected to cancellation. Why did Turnair require such drastic treatment, especially since the records containing the required statistics were at the time in the hands of the RCMP due to the investigation by the CTC of another carrier? The details of that investigation were mentioned a moment ago by the Hon. Member for Regina West.
There may be no change in facts here, but the arbitrary and capricious manner in which the CTC exercised its discretion against a northern Canadian demands review. Who knows the procedures the agency followed which caused it to single out Mr. Turner and cancel his licence? I do not know, and I am sure very few people, if any know. Should a person who has lost his rights to earn a livelihood not know? Should we all not know? Yet Mr. Turner's requests for review were denied.
The result, sadly, is that Turner and his company are financially ruined. A year after the cancellation order, the Privy Council properly reinstated his licence. However, a year out of business caused the loss of all his business assets. He has
National Transportation Act, 1986
begun a suit in the Federal Court but I understand he does not have the funds to complete it. In fact, as of August 2 of this year, Turner will have his home seized by the Royal Bank in Yellowknife.
Ironically, even if Turner had the funds to proceed in the courts, the CTC is claiming that no claim against it can be brought. It insists that Mr. Turner's remedies are limited to review and appeal processes within the agency regulations, including an appeal to the Governor in Council and to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). Any honest, hardworking citizen like Fred Turner should have the right to appeal to an ultimate authority when an agency like the CTC is about to bankrupt him. Bill C-18 must include review processes which are effective and accessible when grounds for review exist. Limiting these grounds only increases the potential for "Fred Turner treatment" of other regulated individuals anywhere in the land. Availability of review, I submit, is necessary to uphold the principles of natural justice under which an administrative agency is obliged to act. In my view, Madam Speaker, all Hon. Members should vote for the amendment now before us.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to rise at this time to support the proposed amendment to Clause 41 because I also believe that the review powers of the new transportation agency created by Bill C-18 should be changed so that a decision of the new agency might be reviewed, rescinded of varied at the discretion of the agency without the need to limit the scope of this review to very specific circumstances. I too believe it is imperative that the agency be able to review as it sees fit because all Members of the Standing Committee on Transport have experienced that drama through which Mr. Fred Turner is now living.
I believe that the two speakers who rose before me-both the spokesman for the New Democratic Party and the representative of the Progressive Conservative Party-and I speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party we are aware that, faced with the whole administrative apparatus of the Government of Canada, this huge government machinery, it often happens that individual rights are crushed by the heavy government machinery. Mr. Turner's experience speaks for itself, I should think.
This is the case of a man who was the victim of such circumstances that the spirit of the law has been applied by officials with undue vigour and rigour. I am not here to judge the attitude of these officials. I believe they acted consciously with uncommon and perhaps excessive zeal. The aftermath of their decision is that an individual acting in good faith and operating under harsh conditions in Canada's northern regions had his licence revoked, which in turn led his business to bankruptcy. Mr. Turner may have made a few minor mistakes, but the consequences and the sanction are disproportionate. All of us Members of the Standing Committee on Transport felt that the consequences imposed to Mr. Turner are infinitely greater than the negligence or lapse which might have taken

June 16, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
place with respect to the Canadian Transport Commission regulations. We had hope that a settlement agreement might be reached to enable Mr. Turner to resume his operations. This is why I chose to intervene personally in the House last May 15 by presenting a petition on behalf of many people who felt that the Government of Canada had inflicted an extreme injustice on Mr. Fred Turner by wrongfully depriving him of his right to earn a living through the operation of his family business. And the petitioners hoped the Government would appoint an independent arbitrator to investigate the details of this case, thus ensuring a settlement that better reflects the true nature of Mr. Fred Turner's loss. However, this petition received no response from the Government.
I remember, it must have been around the same time, in mid-May, that I asked the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) about what could be done by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to try and find a way to agree on satisfactory compensation for Mr. Turner's loss of business.
We felt, and I say we, in referring to members of the Standing Committee on Transport, a group of Members representing different political factions but nevertheless anxious to find a solution to this problem, Members from all sides of the House, both Government and Opposition, we felt that one possibility would be to appoint an impartial arbitrator. And I think it is unfortunate, in the circumstances, that a way has yet to be found to deal with this flagrant injustice.
Some of our colleagues sent a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), asking him to intervene. The letter was signed by a dozen Members of the House of Commons and Senators who wanted the Prime Minister to intervene, not on the basis of law but of basic elementary justice, and find a way to make an ex gratia payment, with the authorization of Treasury Board, to compensate Mr. Turner. The letter, this petition that was sent to the Prime Minister, read as follows:
We believe the licence cancellation was wrong and unfair. The government apparently shares this opinion since on May 30, 1985, the Governor-in-Council, by order, reinstated Turnair's licence. Furthermore, on March 26, 1986, the Governor-in-Council authorized the payment, on an ex gratia basis, of $15,000 to Mr. Turner. In our view, this financial offer is a recognition by the government that Mr. Turner has suffered financial loss as a result of the Air Transport Committee's decision. This sum, however, does not reflect the magnitude of Mr. Turner's financial loss.
[ Translation]
Unfortunately, the Prime Minister, in his answer to the Members of the House of Commons and the Senators who were the joint senders of the letter, said that the case was now before the courts and would have to be settled by the courts.
Now, I feel that this is the kind of case that should not be settled by the courts. We have here one man whose financial resources have dwindled to practically nothing. How is he going to stand up to the Government apparatus? Obviously, if the Government goes into its legalistic stance and says: "Let
the law take its course, let Mr. Turner go before the courts, let him win his case before the courts", what it will cost the Government of Canada in legal expenses to defend the arbitrary and extreme position of its officials will, as far as I can tell, be a very substantial amount that could otherwise be used to compensate Mr. Turner and give him a chance to start up his airline again.
Why spend this money on legal costs? Why take this legalistic stance, since the Government could perfectly well admit its officials had been overzealous and that Mr. Turner should be given the benefit of the doubt and given a fair break?
1 believe that the proposed amendment, if it is accepted, will give the new agency that is to replace the Canadian Transport Commission greater flexibility to review decisions. I think that with a little more goodwill and a little more discretion on the part of the Canadian Transport Commission, the Turner case could have been reviewed, not by the Government but by the existing Canadian Transport Commission. However, instead of agreeing that officials probably had been too severe in Mr. Turner's case and letting the Canadian Transport Commission revise its decision, the Government says: We can't do that. If Mr. Turner doesn't like it, let him go before the courts.
I think this is not the right approach. And I hope that the new agency will be able to act with far greater discretion and discernment and especially with far more flexibility.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I feel compelled to say a word or two about Mr. Turner's case in order to respond to the Hon. Members who have referred to his case in terms of this particular amendment.
The Turner case is a very complex case, as Hon. Members will appreciate, since it deals with the Canadian Transport Commission which not only has certain powers but has incredible responsibilities which Parliament has pressed upon it by statute in order to protect our fellow citizens. The CTC operates under a set of rules that are imposed upon it. It has the obligation to protect you, Madam Speaker, myself, and our fellow citizens.
The problem with Turnair started under the previous administration, and carried on into the term of the previous Minister of Transport and is now in the hands of the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). The three Ministers tried to do what they felt was fair with respect to the over-all circumstances. However, never has any Minister admitted any question of liability in terms of the conduct of the Government of Canada or the Canadian Transport Commission. Any legal person who has looked into the matter on behalf of the Government, including the Ministers, have come to the conclusion that there was no legal liability.
Notwithstanding that, in order to save the time, the trouble
and the costs of a lawsuit, which costs could amount to tens of
thousands of dollars to the taxpayers of Canada, on a without
June 16, 1987

prejudice basis the Minister said to Mr. Turner, "I am prepared to recommend to my colleagues the sum of $15,000".
When I looked into the matter as the Parliamentary Secretary I explored, on an entirely without prejudice basis and without any admission of liability at all, the possibility that perhaps an increased sum could be considered. Figures of $25,000, $30,000 and $40,000 were used. Mr. Turner started at $2 million and tried to work down from there.
I think Hon. Members have to appreciate that every time there is an air crash in Canada the CTC is attacked for not performing its duties. In the year in which we are talking about with respect to not filing information there were over 200 suspensions sent out. All those companies which received suspensions, with the exception of six, filed the appropriate information. Thus there were six actual suspensions after the sending out of some 200 letters asking for more information. Six companies did not provide the information and were suspended. Mr. Turner and Turnair fell into that category. In the case of Turnair there was no suggestion that there was a safety problem.
I ask Hon. Members to think of this. If the CTC had sent out a letter demanding information which was not provided, there was a crash and people were killed, then where would the CTC be? And where would we be as Members? We would be standing in this House, and quite properly, roasting the CTC for not following the rules and regulations that we ourselves set down in the statute and in the regulations.
I plead with Hon. Members to understand where the CTC is coming from on this. In our society, when an agreement as to liability cannot be achieved, the remedy is to use the courts. Mr. Turner in fact did use the courts. He brought an action for some $2 million, an action in which the Government of Canada has now filed its Statement of Defence.
If in fact Mr. Turner is impecunious, those who have some sympathy for his situation should look to assisting him in engaging a lawyer, who can then look at the liability and negotiate on a "without prejudice" basis with the lawyers for the Government of Canada.

The Agency may review, rescind or vary any decision or order made by it or
may rehear any application before deciding it-
That would be all that would be left after the NDP amendment, if it were accepted. Clause 41 continues:
-if, in the opinion of the Agency, since the decision or order or the hearing of

Surely there would have to be some change in the facts or the circumstances such that the agency would be convinced that a rehearing was in order.
With great respect to my friend from Regina West, I would rather have the clause as worded. Any change in the facts or circumstances could be used as justification by the agency for a rehearing.

"(6) A notice of the submission to the Agency under subsection (1) shall be publicized, specifying the name of the shipper, the name of the carrier, the commodity and the origin and destination of the movements, and providing 30 days for interested parties to make submissions to the Agency before any decision is made on whether the matter should proceed under arbitration or should be investigated by the Agency pursuant to section 59."
He said: Madam Speaker, these three motions have to do with the final offer arbitration clauses. In all three motions we are attempting to provide additional reasons why the agency shall not allow for final arbitration. That is, Motion No. 27 relates to the number of reasons a shipper may feel captive and, therefore, eligible for final offer arbitration.
Many transportation companies have expressed the concern that this is a shippers' Bill. I think they are partly right, because it allows shippers to force transportation companies to cut their own throats when there is no one else around prepared to do it.
The problem is that the phrase "captive shippers" originated many years ago when there was little or no trucking industry and when there was no air cargo or air transport industry. Therefore, a shipper was a captive of one railroad. Nowadays a shipper might have only one railroad, but he has 50 trucking companies which are available to transport his goods and/or air cargo or air express services.
I think the term "captive shipper" is badly over-used. Quite frankly, there are shippers claiming captive status who should not have the nerve to claim it any more.
Motion No. 31 amends the clause which insists that the shipper guarantee movement and abide by the arbitrator's decision prior to the arbitration beginning. Surely that must be backwards. Government drafters blew it on that one.
That is all very well, except the customer really dictates whether or not the goods shall move. Because the customer is not and cannot be a party to the arbitration, the amendment would allow for a bona fide offer to move the goods. The assumption is that if the deal falls through, it will not be due to bad faith on the part of the parties to the operation.
Motion No. 31 is particularly important to small shippers, and the transportation critic of the Official Opposition Party also mentioned it. It concerns a company called Prairie Malt which handles malting barley and supplies a number of organizations in the country that bottle stuff for football and baseball games. It is of particular significance for small shippers.
A large shipper which moves thousands of carloads or truckloads per year is in a position to make a very good deal with a transporter, whether it is a railway or a trucking company. However, the small shipper which might only ship from 50 to 200 carloads will not get the same kind of deal.
Motion No. 32 opens up the amount of information available about an arbitration; more information would be available. The assumption is that if there is enough public

knowledge, other competitive solutions will be brought forward and other interested parties would at least know that an arbitration is ongoing.
We are proposing to open up the final arbitration process, upon which the Government insists in the Bill, in terms of information available. We are trying to make an even balance between the interest of the shipper and the interest of the transporter, which would give the arbitrator even more solid ground on which to make a decision.
We think these motions would improve the legislation. We have consulted with numerous organizations and individuals who have asked the Government for these amendments. I hope the Government will decide that they are acceptable.

Madam Speaker, I wish to take part in this debate to express the concern of the Liberal Party about the whole section on arbitration contained in Bill C-18.
We had expressed reservations about these provisions in Committee since it seemed obvious, as we tried to show the Government, that there was a weakness in the new procedure under which, if a shipper is dissatisfied with the rates applied or proposed by a carrier or the conditions associated with the movement of his goods and there is no possibility of an agreement between the shipper and the carrier, the matter can be referred to the Agency for arbitration.
It seems to us that this procedure will become extremely costly, especially as the inevitable consequence of Clause 48 will be that such matters will be negotiated before the arbitrator by legal representatives. It would be unthinkable that railroad companies and those who oppose their proposals go before the arbitrator themselves to make their own representations.
This will give lawyers and law firms throughout the country a lot of business, and shippers, who were expecting that the new procedure would reduce their transport costs, will see very quickly their legal fees increase by 500 per cent. What they gain thanks to lower shipping costs, they will probably lose in higher legal fees.
In my opinion, this arbitration proposal, which could have been interesting, will very quickly become a very costly procedure which will make no one happy. In fact, the arbitrator will have considerable power to determine in the last instance the transport rates for products and goods and the conditions under which carriers will deal with their customers.
Such intervention by a third party in the process seems extremely dangerous to me. We can hope that the chosen arbitrators will be experts who do a faultless job, but I am not at all certain that such will be the case. I believe that no one is better qualified to judge these matters than the employees of the transport companies or the administrators of shipping companies who work on the field and know exactly what is going on.

I would like to underline one last time to the Elouse that this whole arbitration process seems extremely dangerous to me, and I suspect that, within a few years, we shall have to repair the damage done by this procedure as it is not one of the better ideas of this Government.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, last Friday, June 13, two years after the Canadian Jobs Strategy began, the Government finally saw the light and changed the program to permit greater participation by immigrant and native women.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
June 16, 1987
Why is the Government going only halfway? Why keep this inflexible entry rule at all? What about all those people who are out of work and need training but have not yet been unemployed for 24 weeks? Must they wait around for five or six months before they get help? Or must they continue to accept unskilled, part-time, short term and low pay employment? CREATION OF JOBS THROUGHOUT COUNTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since September, 1984, when Canadians opted for sound economic management, some 840,000 jobs have been created in Canada.
The best the critics can do to detract from this good news is to say that all the jobs are in Ontario. The fact is the jobs are spread around. There are 388,000 in Ontario, 220,000 in Quebec, 92,000 in British Columbia, and 50,000 in the Atlantic region. Even on the Prairies, despite record low grain, oil, potash and uranium prices there are 88,000 more people working.
Wherever the jobs are in Canada, 1 applaud the Government for creating an environment in which private sector initiative and entrepreneurship have been able to put over 840,000 more Canadians to work.
I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for the success of their economic policies which have given all Canadians greater access to more jobs regardless of where they live.

CRITICISM OF PROVISIONS OF BILL C-55
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, CLC President Shirley Carr sent a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) two weeks ago calling Bill C-55, the Government's refugee legislation, a betrayal of trust and a mockery of fundamental rights. Flaws she noted were denial of universal access, denial of appeal, and denial of those coming from so-called safe countries such as Central Americans applying from the U.S. She also objected to the philosophy of the Bill which blames refugees for problems in the refugee determination system and seems designed to keep refugees out of Canada.
At the same time, a telex from spokespersons for the Anglican, Baptist, Christian Reformed, Mennonite, Presbyterian, United and Roman Catholic Churches, along with
the Religious Society of Friends, the Salvation Army, and the Canadian Council of Churches, made the same points. They said "The Bill is being promoted on the false premise that it will protect genuine refugees. It is clear that the effect of this Bill will be to turn away refugees."
"The 'alleged abuse', which is the pretext for this flawed piece of legislation, is primarily the result of prolonged government delays in reforming the present drawn-out and cumbersome procedure." They demand a Bill to help refugees.

SIZE OF CORPORATION'S DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, judging by the just released 1986 annual report of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation it has evidently been living through some very interesting times. Highlights are the $1.25 billion deficiency in the deposit insurance fund and the $1 billion loan from the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
The corporation estimates that even with no new demands on the insurance fund it will take until 1994 to eliminate the deficit with the current one-tenth of 1 per cent premium rate. Therefore, whether we like it or not, there is no real alternative except to approve the provisions of Bill C-42 which would authorize increased premium rates and a higher ceiling on government lending to the corporation.

In 1932, Mr. Speaker, a group of Canadians, significantly linked through geographical circumstances, decided to establish a political Party, the Canadian Commonwealth Federation, or CCF. From 1932 to 1961, Party activists could not manage to develop principles, let alone national programs. Opportunism being their forte, they attempted to fool the people by changing the name of their Party, not a particularly challenging initiative when the name does not reflect the truth.
From the smoking ashes of the CCF sprang the NDP in 1961. The activists of this Party have yet to set forth a major policy. Their opportunism has taught them to change on a daily basis to mirror the colour of the day. The only qualifier which would fit every last one of them, their leader included, is the word socialist. How else could anyone appear at the International Socialist convention under another hat?
Since the Rhinoceros Party is now defunct, another rare, and excentric animal whose colours match the surrounding foliage should be their inspiration in the quest for a new name, the Chameleon Party.

REPRESENTATION OF CLIENTS BY ARRESTED IMMIGRATION CONSULTANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and his Department for initiating action against those so-called immigration consultants whose specialty is to prey on human misery. These individuals have caused untold human suffering within the Portuguese community by promising unsuspecting individuals an easy road to becoming landed immigrants. Thus the Minister's action was thoroughly endorsed and appreciated by the Portuguese community.
However, the positive aspects of the action are beginning to fade. Two days after the arrests took place Joe Raphael, one of the consultants charged and an individual who is notorious for counselling people to circumvent Canadian immigration law, was again representing clients in front of the Immigration Appeal Board.
By continuing to represent clients Mr. Raphael is continuing to project the image that he is above the law and can deliver on any immigration matter. Until their cases are heard a cease and desist order should be issued against these individuals. The Government must make it clear that no immigration consultant is above the law.

speechtext:

NEED TO UPGRADE TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week the Canadian Construction Association called for $500 million annually of federal assistance to highway construction.
This call is timely in view of the poor state of our highways, especially the Trans-Canada Highway through northern Ontario.
The call also follows on some federal recognition of responsibility for highway improvement in Atlantic Canada, Quebec and the western provinces. Every province except Ontario now has an agreement with the federal Government on highways improvement.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has not, however, responded favourably to requests I have made, as has the Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry), to assist the Province of Ontario in the upgrading and twinning of the Trans-Canada Highway through northern Ontario.
Northern Ontario contains one-quarter of the total length of the Trans-Canada Highway. The Province of Ontario is only now beginning to recognize its responsibility to make this a first-class highway.
I call upon the Minister of Transport to respond favourably to Ontario's request for federal assistance for improvement of our Trans-Canada Highway.

PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND NATIONAL PARK-SUGGESTED RENAMING OF RUSTICO ISLAND AS ROBINSON ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the ideas behind establishing National Parks in Canada was to maintain our country's and our people's heritage.
Rustico Island, in Prince Edward Island National Park, should rightfully be called Robinson Island, after the Robinson family who purchased, settled, and farmed it in 1815.
The Robinson family had been on Prince Edward Island since 1778, arriving there with other Loyalists from the United States. While many of those Loyalists returned to England, the Robinson family stayed, and worked long and hard to develop their island, their province and their country.
The island the Robinsons settled was known as Robinson Island until the Government took over the land now known as the National Park. Even after the National Park was established, the Island was known to most as Robinson Island. In fact the 1968 official road map of Prince Edward Island refers to that island as Robinson Island.
It is only fitting that Rustico Island should once again be called Robinson Island in honour of the family who pioneered it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the
present time, the Railway Act prohibits railway companies and
June 16, 1987

shippers from concluding confidential contracts for the transportation of goods by rail in Canada.
According to Section 275 of the Act, tariffs are to be published and filed with the Canadian Transport Commission, and Section 269 provides that railway companies shall charge only the tolls specified in the tariffs.
According to Section 381, any departure from such tolls would be an offence under the Act.
And finally, under Section 380, granting unpublished rebates would be an offence.
Madam Speaker, these conditions differ very sustantially from those existing in the United States since the Staggers Rail Act was adopted in 1980. This legislation authorizes U.S. railway companies to engage in confidential contracting with shippers.
As we know, this situation has harmed Canada's railway companies competing for transborder traffic with U.S. railway companies. The latter were in a position to offer better rates than those published in Canada and were thus able to short-circuit Canadian railway companies by detouring traffic through the United States. The previous Government became aware of the situation and asked the Canadian Transport Commission to look into the matter and make recommendations.
At hearings before the Transport Committee, most witnesses were in favour of the concept of confidential contracting for transborder traffic, in order to make up for the weakness in the existing regulatory system. When the question was being studied by the Canadian Transport Commission, experts reached the same conclusion. Something had to be done to keep U.S. railway companies from having an edge over Canadian railway companies in the area of transborder traffic.
The solution was entirely in line with the views of the previous Liberal Government, and that is what we need, no more. Unfortunately, the present Conservative Government wanted to go much further. Here again, it was led by its constant urge to follow the U.S. model in every respect, to copy everything that is being done south of the border.
The Government has extended confidential contracting to domestic traffic, thereby copying the U.S. Staggers Rail Act. We in the Liberal Party do not favour confidential contracting on domestic traffic, because we feel that such contracting will soon become a barrier to healthy competition. It will certainly not be in the interests of the small and average shipper. It will put the Atlantic provinces at a disadvantage and be a serious threat to the trucking industry in Canada, especially in the long-haul east-west sector. And we also believe that with the introduction of domestic confidential contracts, the railway freight companies will try to recover the business lost as a result of increased competition in this sector and do so at the expense of the small "captive" shippers.
We think that drumming up business at the expense of small and average "captive" shippers, which will benefit the big
National Transportation Act, 1986
conglomerates that are free to do as they please, is totally unacceptable. I have said so before and I say it again, Madam Speaker, that we are not alone in this respect. A number of interveners, who testified before the Standing Committee of the House of Commons that examined these clauses, objected to the preferential treatment the Conservative Government wants to give the big Canadian shippers. Several interveners told us that a system that would allow confidential contracting on domestic traffic would have disastrous repercussions.

In fact, in one of the most compelling representations before the Committee, a small Saskatchewan malt producer, Prairie Malt Limited, of Biggar, told us that the Staggers Act has resulted in disastrous consequences for those shippers not large or powerful enough to compete effectively with the larger and more powerful conglomerates.
I want to quote part of the submission that was presented:
To give the Staggers Act its credits due, it must also be mentioned that larger corporations, holding a dominant position within their given industrial sector on account of size and general financial and economic clout, are more than satisfied with the law as it stands.
In consequence, efficient, but economically weaker or geographically disadvantaged competitors within the industry can be driven out with comparative ease, since they are not able to wield the same amount of influence with the railways as larger corporations with their widely dispersed interests and plant sites.
Confidential contracting could allow the larger, more powerful shippers not only an advantage over smaller competitors, but also to utilize transportation contracts and through them the railways themselves to literally push out the competition.

And according to the Minister of Transport himself, this legislation on deregulation is aimed at boosting competition. Well, here is a small shipper who is telling us that, far from increasing, competition will decrease.
One of the other most flagrant shortcomings of this legislation and of this part of the law is the fact that it throws the doors of the Canadian market wide open to the American railway companies, yet the Staggers Rail Act does not include similar provisions. It is quite clear that these clauses are detrimental to Canadian railway companies.

This kind of one-way free trade that the Government favours is totally unacceptable to us. We in the Opposition have tried to bring amendments to protect the Canadian interests and Canadian railways from the unfair competition by the American railways that will be possible.
Under the confidential contracting provisions currently in this legislation, we will see a situation where American railways could run freight in Canada based on confidential contracting on trans-border traffic. Burlington Northern, for instance-

Madam Speaker, I want to speak to four motions, two moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), and two moved by myself.
Motion No. 37 is designed so that in conducting investigations under Clause 59 on a matter of public interest, investigators will not be frustrated by secret information but would be allowed access to that information. Under the provisions of the Bill presently before the House, someone who investigates a confidential contract would not have access to all the confidential information.
In Motions Nos. 60 and 62, the Hon. Member for Papineau has expressed views we can support. I believe the Chair has ruled that an affirmative vote on Motion No. 63 obviates the need to put the questions on Motions Nos. 60 and 61, which means the vote on Motion No. 63 must be called first. A negative vote on Motion No. 63 then means that Motions Nos. 60 and 61 must be voted on.
My Motion No. 63 deletes the entire clause of the Bill referring to confidential contracts. I never thought I would live to see the day where a Progressive Conservative Government, which advocates private enterprise, market forces, competition, and so on, would bring in measures which are anti-competitive. It means that those with corporate power, whether railroads, trucking companies or airlines, or those large shippers who ship thousands and thousands of carloads or truck loads a year, can get a confidential contract. But a company such as Prairie
Malt Limited in Biggar, Saskatchewan-and there are thousands like it all over the country-which may ship a few dozen or a few hundred carloads or truck loads, do not get the same deal as the large shippers. Anyone in this House who thinks they do is dreaming in technicolour. It is an anticompetitive provision. I do not understand why the Government would hold still for a confidential contract.
Even on an appeal on a confidential contract, the poor shipper who thinks the other guy has a confidential contract with a railroad or trucking company, has no choice under this Bill but to automatically appeal. But he cannot find out because it is confidential. Not even the investigators can find out. What kind of an appeal is that? What kind of natural justice is that?
The primary amendment in that grouping of four motions is to delete the entire section on confidential contracts. We should be enlarging, enforcing and playing a watch-dog role- and by that I mean a Government agency or the Department of Transport-on the system of agreed charges. Any shipper, large or small, who agrees, for example, to ship 75 per cent of his traffic by a certain carrier should be eligible for that reduced rate. The same opportunity should apply to every shipper. In order to get that rate all he has to do is to agree to ship a certain percentage of his traffic and it can start at 100 per cent or 50 per cent because there is a graduated rate. Those agreed charges should be public information. Every shipper, large or small, would then have exactly the same opportunity.
The bureaucrats in the nether regions of the Department of Transport have dreamed this clause up at the request of the largest shippers in the country, and it flies in the face of one of the underlying principles of the Bill, that is, regional economic expansion. The small manufacturers, processors and shippers in Atlantic Canada, out west or in northern Ontario are automatically ruled out when it comes to confidential contracts. There is no way any so-called self-respecting private enterprise government which believes in free market forces would put confidential contracts into its legislation.
When one is dealing with a public utility, a public service or with a transporter, confidential contracts should be equally available to every shipper and passenger in this country. They should not be discriminated against because of their size, where they happen to be located, where they happen to be producing their goods or where they happen to be travelling from or to. To use the language of the Reaganites over here, that should be a "level playing field". Small shippers, people who travel from small and middle sized locations in Canada, should have the same opportunity for discount fares, seat sales or anything else offered by an airline. This Bill should require every transporter to make available the same opportunities to every shipper, every receiver, every passenger, no matter where they live.
The Government flies in the face of its own free enterprise,
free market forces principles. Why would it not want a small
shipper, manufacturer or processor in Atlantic Canada to have

an equal opportunity of access to competitive or compensatory rates as the large shipper in downtown Toronto or Montreal? Why would one want legislation which would prohibit that? 1 do not understand the Government.
Surely to goodness Motion No. 63 which would delete the entire clause dealing with confidential contracts would-and as a democratic socialist I hate to be helpful to the proponents of free enterprise market forces across the way-help the Government out. It would reinforce and restate the principles for which Members opposite claim to stand. It is a heck of a note when a democratic socialist has to give lessons to free enterprisers about sound business practices and about treating people across the country in exactly the same way no matter where they live.
Surely that is what this legislation should do. No one should be discriminated against. This is something which Canada has tried to do since 1881 to ensure that transportation is distributed in a reasonably equitable manner no matter where one lives. We have not reached that goal but we have proceeded along the way to reaching it. Confidential contracts fly in the face of our history. They fly in the face of the so-called principles and policies of the Progressive Conservative Party.
This is a crucial area of this legislation. I do not know of any self-respecting Progressive Conservative in my City of Regina-as few as they are-who is in favour of these confidential contracts. I do not know one. In fact, they want a fair shake. When they are bidding against someone in Winnipeg, Toronto or Vancouver for freight rates they want to have an equal chance.
The small implement manufacturers in the prairie provinces come to mind in this regard. There are about two dozen of them who ship a few hundred truckloads or carloads a year. If anyone on the government side thinks that they can compete with J. I. Case, Massey-Ferguson or International Harvester, which companies ship thousands of carloads a year, then they are discriminating against the small farm implement manufacturers in western Canada.
The same applies to every commodity that can be named when it comes to the difference between the economic, power, clout and influence as between a small processor and manufacturer and a large one. Confidential contracts are an anathema to this Party. They should be an anathema to anyone who believes in a free society, a free chance, an equal chance, an equal opportunity.
I wish that Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier were here today to see the actions of this Government and its Reaganomic nonsense which fly in the face of everything the country has been trying to do since 1867. Members opposite are hypnotized. They have not thought the process through. They do not know what the hell they are doing.

Motion No. 63 must be accepted. It will obviate debate on the other three amendments. Failing that, let us adopt the other three.

Madam Speaker, perhaps 1 may also make a short contribution to the debate on these motions, to try and explain the position of our Party. We are in favour of confidential contracting for transborder traffic, so that Canadian railway companies, including Canadian National and Canadian Pacific, can compete with U.S. railway companies who, at the present contracts. But that is where our generosity ends, because we object to confidential contracting on domestic traffic. I think the testimomy heard by the Transport Committee was practically unanimous on the point that big shippers would benefit from confidential contracting. In fact, we would see a rather bizarre situation where small shippers would actually be subsidizing the conglomerates that would most certainly benefit from the price war resulting from confidential contracting.
I must say this is a distressing possiblity for the regions, both in eastern and western Canada. I would like to point out that once again, witnesses from the Atlantic provinces testified before the Standing Committee on Transport that the economy of their part of the country is based to a large extent on the small business sector. The people of the Atlantic provinces believe that through a form of cross-subsidization, their part of the country might very well be forced to subsidize the low-cost confidential contracts resulting from the cheap rates that would be charged in central Canada.
The Government of Alberta had similar concerns about the impact of confidential contracting on western Canada.

I would have a question, Madam Speaker, for the proponents of these confidential contracts. As I understand it, when it comes to matters of public transportation, tariffs have always been posted. Why is there a need for confidential contracts? What is the motivation?
I can certainly understand the reasons for giving a large shipper a preferential rate, or for coming to a special arrangement with a large shipper of merchandise. There certainly are economies of scale that a larger shipper can benefit from in negotiating lower shipping rates, particularly if that shipper is able to get the goods to the departure point, thus permitting the railways to avoid some of the costs that they have to assume when it comes to picking up small pieces of merchandise from different parts of the country.
Why should the contracts be confidential? Why should they not be public? Why should other shippers not be able to become aware of the nature and contents of the contracts so as, perhaps, to be able to organize their affairs in a similar fashion, and hope to benefit from the same advantageous treatment if they are able to do so? It seems to me that this is the way in which a free and open market should operate.
The burden of proof should be on the proponents of these confidential contracts. From what I have heard in the debate

We have the rather bizarre situation where the Government is almost down on its hands and knees offering all kinds of advantages to the Americans in the hope that at some point we will be rewarded for our generosity. He said: Madam Speaker, if there was ever a crux of this legislation, it is these two amendments about which Members from all sides of the House have shown and expressed concern. It deals with the safety of airline operations and the capability and capacity of airline operators and aircraft operators to meet those standards on which the Government itself has said there will be no compromise. Our amendments attempt to and we believe will ensure those standards of safety.
Motion No. 44 requires that a new licensing agency must look at the ability of a new carrier to meet high safety standards before a licence is issued. That has been one of the problems until now.
As I informed the House earlier today, Motion No. 21A is what I call the Fred Turner amendment. There are licensed carriers now operating without a valid operating certificate. Those certificates are testimony from Transport Canada that it is satisfied with the carriers' level of safety and maintenance. It is my understanding that when this House brought in the new amendments to the Aeronautics Act in 1985, a direct link between economic licence and the operating authority was inadvertently broken. I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to pay close attention. That broken link means, as we have seen, that an air carrier can retain its licence and operate while having no operating certificate. This morning I referred to the crash at Schefferville in which eight people were killed. The airline's operating authority had been suspended in October of 1983, but it was operating on September 30, 1985, when these tragic fatalities occurred. Even today that airline still does not have a valid operating certificate. It has a licence to fly but no certificate. There are other carriers operating today without that certificate. If the Government is serious about safety, this House will adopt Motion No. 44 and Motion No. 2 because they go to the very heart of what the Government itself said was a fundamental principle of this Bill.

You cannot have people operating airlines and carrying passengers without authority to do so. Yet they are doing it now. I do not care whether it is Wapiti or Spur airlines or this airline in Schefferville which I understand now has a new name.
If the Government wants deregulation, if it wants complete ease of exit and entry, all right, that is government policy. I do not like it, but so what? However, no Government worthy of the name can allow any airline to operate without proper safety, maintenance and pilot checks. The problem is that the air traffic committee of the CTC has one licensing authority and the Department of Transport, under the Aeronautics Act, has another. The two do not get together. We cannot allow that to continue.
This airline in Schefferville killed eight people and we did not cancel its licence. Yet poor old Fred Turner in Yellowknife is late filing his reports about gasoline used and the number of passengers carried and his licence is cancelled. He went bankrupt and lost five aircraft and is now losing his house. That cannot be justified under any circumstances. We cannot allow people a licence to fly and give them authority to carry passengers until they have met all the standards which this Government says must be met regarding safety and maintenance. That has to be in place before we pass this Bill.
This motion acknowledges the fact that we are all concerned about safety and maintenance. There are also other areas we should be concerned about. Bill C-19 should not be passed until the new national safety code is in place. Bill C-18 should not be passed until the new national rail safety rules are in place. Both those Bills should not be passed until all the boards, agencies, regulations and inspectors dealing with licensing, safety, security and maintenance are set up. Then if you want to deregulate and let anyone and everyone go in and out of air, trucking or railway operations, they will at least have to meet certain standards. Until they do, you do not give them a licence.
My hon. friend from Prince George, who flies in the north quite a lot, knows whereof I speak. I have been on some of these jerkwater outfits that fly with a minimum of maintenance, pilots who are flying extra hours because if they do not the boss fires them. I am not a white-knuckle flier but I do not want any amateurs or anyone played out, or a plane which is unfit, carrying me anywhere in this country.
The Government can do no less than accept these amendments. They do not do violence to the basic principles of the Bill dealing with deregulation, competition and market forces. Therefore, I hope my friends opposite will persuade the Parliamentary Secretary to get up and say he accepts them both.

Madam Speaker, the amendment now under consideration allows us to focus on the hypocrisy of this Government. Every time we have spoken about safety, the current Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and his predecessor have told us that the Government had no intention of jeopardizing transport safety in Canada. All that we have had are nice speeches. The Minister of Transport and his officials have never taken any specific action to ensure that safety will not be jeopardized.
This amendment would simply add to the the interpretation provisions of the National Transportation Act the principle of striving for the highest possible standards of safety.
Yet, the Government is refusing to approve this amendment, thus proving its insincerity as it does not want to spell out in the objectives of the new National Transportation Act that there will be an effort to provide the highest possible standards of safety for transport services in Canada. If the Government is not willing to accept this amendment, it should not try to make the population believe that it wants to protect the safety of travellers as it is refusing to take the necessary action to ensure this safety.
I have here a report prepared by the Clerk's Office of the City of Toronto, which report was submitted to the members of the Standing Committee on Transport and is quite symptomatic of what people think of the desire of this Government to hasten passage of a law which will radically transform transportation in Canada and certainly jeopardize the safety of our transportation system.
If I may, Madam Speaker, I would like to quote a few passages from the brief submitted to the Government and to the Standing Committee on Transport during its consideration of Bill C-18, and I quote:
While a lot of the concerns raised by these Bills deal with the loss of services in small communities and remote areas, this transportation policy will also adversely affect major transportation centres such as Metro Toronto. First, safety risks will increase because of more flexible entry standards and the absence of detailed and adequate inspection mechanisms.
As the Metro Toronto Residents Action Committee stated in its submission to the Standing Committee on Transport of the Canadian Parliament in November, the lack of specific provisions dealing with public safety is one of the major weeknesses in the Freedom to Move position paper. In the United States, where transportation has been deregulated for nine years, there has been a significant drop in public safety. The number of accidents has increased on American highways, because the equipment is used more often with less maintenance, and truck drivers work longer shifts and haul heavier loads than they used to.
The Committee mentions a whole series of statistics showing a significant increase in the number of accidents and crashes which have been taking place on U.S. highways since the transportation system was deregulated.
The submission goes on with these words:

In the city of Toronto, safety concerns are of a double nature: the transport of dangerous goods. It is a cause for deep concern in densely populated areas such as Toronto where huge quantities of chemicals and other dangerous goods are transported every day by rail, by truck and by plane. People realized the threat of disasters with the Mississauga derailment which forced evacuation for six days of some 225,000 people. That accident is probably at the origin of the submission by the City of Toronto to the federal Government urging that any reform of the transport sector should clearly state that safety must be a top priority item and that an inquiry board directly responsible to Parliament should be created. However, the Government has not followed up on those recommendations. It has ignored the briefs submitted first to the Government following the publication of the Freedom to Move document, and later on in connection with the study of Bill C-18, which is not specifically concerned with the basic problem of safety.
That is why the Opposition wants to have that amendment. That is why the Liberal Party tried in committee to move an amendment to this bill which was rejected by the Conservative majority in the committee. And that is also why I support wholeheartedly this amendment standing in the name of my colleague from the New Democratic Party, and which is to ensure-that is no big deal- that there is clear recognition in the new National Transportation Act of the fact that in those national transportation targets, the highest possible safety standards will be specified. That the Government is unwilling to accept that goal is to me illogical, incomprehensible and certainly unjustified.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I want to continue the debate on a very important aspect of the process which we are going through as well as on the final wording of Bill C-18. The purpose of the two motions standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is to ensure that there is recognition within the Bill of safety in a context which is not found elsewhere in the legislation.
During our hearings on Bill C-18, and when we were dealing with the Government's White Paper Freedom to Move, one of the areas on which my colleague and I focused in considerable detail was safety, particularly air safety. We tended to ask the witnesses who appeared before us their opinion on what faces the last passenger on the final flight of an airline company that is going bankrupt. For instance, how many corners have been cut in the maintenance of the aircraft and how many times during the week had the pilot been forced to fly longer than humanly reasonable? Did the company overlook mechanical problems? Was it carrying out maintenance to the minimum standard as opposed to keeping maintenance safely within government and industry specifications?
As a result of our deliberations we concluded that in a system in which there is no guarantee of economic survival and the market-place forces the owners of the company to stretch resources continually, that safety could be compromised by an operator who, perhaps not intentionally, was forced to take unnecessary risks due to the aggressive competition within the industry. Such risks might include such requests as asking the pilot to fly one or two hours longer, to asking the mechanic to turn a blind eye on certain repairs that may not be mandatory but could be crucial in the event of a problem.
Motions Nos. 44 and 2 attempt to meet those concerns. Motion No. 44 basically adds to the requirement for domestic service. Clause 71(1) states:
A person shall not operate a domestic service unless, in respect of that
service,
(a)	holds a domestic licence;
(b)	holds a Canadian aviation document; and
(c)	has prescribed liability insurance coverage.
Motion No. 44 would change Clause 71(1)(b) to read:
(b) holds a Canadian aviation document, and has demonstrated the
capability and the willingness to meet the highest possible standards of
safety;
We believe that amendment will accomplish a number of
things. First, when a group applies for a certain certificate in

June 16, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
order to operate a domestic service, not only must it prove that it has liability insurance and a domestic licence, it must also have a proven track record for safety and the capability and willingness to meet the highest possible standards of safety.
One might ask how a new entrant can have a proven track record. One of the most ludicrous suggestions we heard in the committee was that the banks should decide whether or not a new airline company is healthy and has the proper equipment and safety and maintenance procedures in place. I suggest that it is the responsibility of the Government to ensure the protection of the people who use those services which are approved or authorized by the Government.
This amendment will require the agency to consider all new applicants and determine whether or not they have the resources not only today but in the future to maintain their standard of service and employment for an extended period of time. It must not be a company that provides such working conditions and wages as to have a continual turnover of personnel.
We have seen examples of such "fly-by-nighters", as my colleagues refers to them. These companies seem to have a continual turnover of pilots because of poor working conditions and low wages, which means that people with little experience are piloting these aircraft.
There must be a system in place so that the Government, through its agency, can determine not only whether those carriers are safe on the day the licences are issued but will remain safe because they have the economic wherewithal to maintain their services to the flying public.
That stability existed under the old regulated regime in which there was built in cross-subsidization. A carrier could be assured of a reasonable return on its investment in less lucrative runs and therefore not be forced into making economic decisions that could ultimately lead to disaster. Earlier, my colleague referred to a report from the Canadian Aviation Safety Board in a letter of June 15 in response to an inquiry from the Member's staff person regarding an aircraft accident in Schefferville, Quebec, in September, 1985.
I have a copy of the investigation report and engineering report LP250/85. The covering letter indicated that the aircraft in question did not have a valid operating authority. In fact, it had been suspended in October, 1983.
Clearly, there are carriers who are not qualified to be operating. We believe that this amendment will help to ensure that there are no blind spots left between the aviation safety legislation and the National Transportation Act. I urge the Government seriously to consider accepting this amendment. If our wording is not totally acceptable to the Government, perhaps there is a way in which the clause can stand until later so that it can be studied. If that is not possible, I look forward to hearing the Government's response to this amendment.

Madam Speaker, Motion No. 49 is a trigger mechanism which would prevent an air carrier from doing itself in. In the United States we saw a great deal of cutthroat competition in which fares were slashed and safety was jeopardized. Fares were slashed to such an extent that service for those who travelled on the
airlines slashing them was very poor. This put the carriers into a risky financial situation and ultimately lead to their bankruptcies and mergers with other air carriers.
Motion No. 49 might be perceived by consumers as being unpopular or unfair to them since everyone wants this great break, a 50 per cent reduction in air fares. We just saw a situation last week in which Canadian Airlines International announced a very unusual seat sale for the summer months to a number of Canadian centres at a time when volumes are normally high. It left out a number of communities, including Thunder Bay. Through its policy of automatically matching where possible challenges in terms of seat sales by Canadian Airlines International Air Canada, CAIL's only competitor decided to match CAIL. It did not propose to provide service to Thunder Bay.
If this amendment were accepted by the Government in an instance where there is more than a 50 per cent reduction in basic fares, air carriers would have to apply to the agency for permission. The agency would then be able to say: "First, yes, because of the size of the airline you can afford to do this, but not very often. Second, you have to be fair to all of Canada. You cannot just offer this seat sale in areas where you are planning to offer it. You have to make sure that communities such as Thunder Bay also have the advantage of these cheap seats".
That is what this Bill was supposed to give to the people of Canada-cheap transportation, even though we have been told time and time again by the experts in the field and by the carriers themselves that by and large we have bottomed out and all we have to look forward to are higher fares in the future with the odd aberration such as a seat sale. At the very least it would ensure that if a company is prepared to provide that type of break, then the agency would be in a position to review it to ensure economic stability as well as fairness.
