speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the existing regulatory system, Section 276 of the Railway Act requires that all railway freight rates be compensatory. The purpose of this provision is to protect shippers and competitors of railway companies, whose commercial interests might be harmed by non-competitive activities.
This provision aims at ensuring fair and loyal intermodal competition.
Essentially, Section 276 of the Railway Act aims at giving some protection to companies such as the ACE Inc. Maritime Transport Company which have suffered from unfair competition on the part of the railways. This company provides container maritime transport services between Central Canada and Newfoundland and is thus in direct competition with the Terra Transport Division of the CNR.
In 1979, the Canadian Government gave the CN $77 million to transform its railway car transport system into a container service. As soon as the containers became operational in 1982, the CN launched a rate war by setting substantially lower rates than its variable costs.
Because of this practice, ACE Inc. had to lower its own prices to the level of the non-compensatory rates set by the CN. Despite its efforts, the company lost many contracts and had to serve many of its remaining customers at a loss.
The company filed a complaint against the tariff practices of the CN as soon as its administrators found that they could not avoid losses on their markets. The complaint filed with the Minister of Transport was referred to the Canadian Transport Commission, which was asked to investigate. The Commission finally established that a large number of the CN's tariffs for Newfoundland were lower than its variable costs, contrary to the provisions of Section 276 of the Railway Act.
ACE Inc. will have lost several million dollars because of its inability to charge rates high enough to cover its costs, due to the CN's harmful tariff practices. It now owes its survival to a subsidy from the Canadian Governement, which recognized the unfairness of the CN's practices and tried to preserve a competitive maritime transport service while the Commission was pursuing its investigation.
June 16, 1987

What Clause 113 of Bill C-18 would do is exempt railroads from applying compensatory rates where they establish that the rate is not significantly reducing competition or eliminating a competitor, and was not designed to have that effect.
In all fairness, we can wonder what purpose the Government had in mind when choosing to abolish the protection afforded by Section 276.
Indeed, in the view of many agencies that appeared before the Committee on Transport, both at the time of the examination of the White Paper Freedom to Move, and during the discussion of Bill C-18, the elimination of provisions ruling out unfair practices makes no economic sense.
The Montreal Chamber of Commerce had this to say on the matter:

"There is no economic motivation for non-compensatory rates but to lessen competition. The law should encourage intermodal competition in a fair and even-handed manner. It should not pit the financial resources of one transportation mode against another."

Moreoever, the present wording puts in doubt the implementation of the clause. Clearly, the new agency would have all the difficulty in the world basing a decision on the working criteria of that clause. I am quoting on that the Luscar Company, which also appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport, and I quote:

"Subsection (5) creates an unnecessary and undesirable exception to the requirement that railway freight rates be compensatory. What constitutes a substantial lessening of competition is not only subjective, but is also an onus that may be easily met. For example, elimination of one competitor or one competitive mode with other competitors or modes remaining may not be deemed to be a substantial lessening of competition. Moreover, competition from other sources may be argued to be a sufficient retention of competition to meet the onus of the Section.
Whether or not a freight rate was designed to limit competition is also subjective. Numerous arguments could ensue relating to whether the rate was a legitimate competitive action or an action that was intended to reduce competition. It is instructive that the only successful predatory pricing complaint under the Combines Investigation Act involved the actual giving away of product by one competitor."

On this side of the House, in the Liberal Party, we are urging retention of Section 276 for three major reasons: It contributes to the railways' financial stability, by preventing them from getting into a price war below compensatory rates; It serves as a verification mechanism in case of prohibitive rates. Finally, it prevents railways from entering into unfair
National Transportation Act, 1986
price competition to the detriment of healthy intermodal competition. Moreover, it is important to emphasize that on that matter, even the Committee on Transport, when reviewing the Freedom to Move document, favoured retaining Section 276. Indeed, in its report Freedom to Move-Change, Choice, Challenge, the Committee had this to say:
Both the trucking industry and CP Rail are particularly concerned that CN Rail might be inclined to price its services below cost to a greater extent than its competitors in the absence of Section 276. They believe that CN enjoys special financial advantages as a Crown corporation as a result of which it would be able to undertake predatory pricing practices.
Several witnesses indicated that in the absence of Section 276, the Combines Investigation Act would not provide sufficient protection.
We agree that this Act is not adequate protection against predatory pricing. Indeed the Committee has concluded that the only effective mechanism currently in place to deter predatory pricing on the part of our railways is Section 276. Therefore, Section 276 should be maintained, and not repealed in five years as proposed by Freedom to Move. We see this as the first of a package of safeguards for shippers and competitors of the railways whose commercial interests might be harmed by anti-competitive behavior when confidential contracts are introduced.
The Committee also feels that clause 276 should be strengthened by providing a new legislation with penalties for the levying of non compensatory rates.
In concluding, I find it rather sad to note that on such a fundamental issue, the Tory members of the Standing Committee on Transport altered their opinion to satisfy the whims of the Minister of Transport. When the paper entitled "Freedom to Move" was considered, they agreed to maintain Clause 276. A few months later, when Bill C-18 was examined, those same Tory members who has suggested that Clause 276 should be maintained, ask us to remove it.
This is the reason why we are asking our colleagues to support this motion which responds to the concerns not only of the Montreal Board of Trade, but also those of the Luscar Company, the ACE Company as well as the Saskatchewan Government, the Canadian Pacific, the Board of Trade of Metropolitan Toronto and many other witnesses who appeared before the Committee on Transport and asked us to have Clause 276 in the current National Transportation Act maintained in Bill C-18.

He said: Madam Speaker, this is one of the crucial parts of the Bill. Some transportation economists have said that it is a licence to raid railway revenues, namely competitive line rates. We urge the Government to accept these amendments.
The first in this group would make certain that a competitive line rate will not be established for a shipper who does not ship a substantial amount of goods by the route in question. In other words, 75 per cent of their 12-month tonnage must go by the route in question.
Motion No. 68 is the crux of the matter. We want the whole competitive line rate section of the Bill deleted.
Failing that, we urge adoption of Motion No. 69. Let me say that trailers and containers on flat cars are not eligible for competitive line rates primarily because the mere presence of the goods in such a container would prove that the goods were not captive and could be transported by truck. This amendment addresses the reality that some goods are captive due to extreme financial costs of other modes when leaving the shipper, but may be delivered by a different mode.
Self-owned containers are the only answer. This amendment would protect truckers from anyone using this section to get the edge on them in the trucking industry. For example, Prairie Malt says that it must ship by rail from their door, but many customers must receive by truck. The conflict in that clause of the Bill passes all understanding. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been a very busy day.
I know that we do not like to negotiate on the floor of the House. However, I was under the impression that with a slight amendment to this clause it would be acceptable to the Government as well as to the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) in whose name this motion stands. The House would be inclined to give agreement to the Hon. Member's motion on the understanding that we would complete Bill C-19 at both stages tonight. I wish to confirm whether or not that is the understanding of the Hon. Member.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have indicated to the Parliamentary Secretary that, indeed, we on this side of the House would be inclined to dispose of report stage of Bill C-19. In fact, this is something that I confirmed with the Hon. Member's Whip in discussions earlier. I regret if the Hon. Member is under the impression that the agreement dealt with both the report stage and the third reading stage. There has been no time allocation motion moved with respect to Bill C-19. The Parliamentary Secretary must understand that he is getting quite a lot already by having us agree to dispose tonight of report stage of Bill C-19. The Government will get third reading tomorrow or the day after. It will be a short debate at third reading. I know that the Government is anxious to expedite this legislation and the Opposition is co-operating. I do not think the Government should ask too much.
Certainly, these amendments which have been presented in good faith should not be the subject of that type of wheeling and dealing. If the Parliamentary Secretary is willing to accept the amendment then he should accept it and we will do our best in relation to debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, subject to the condition that it will be a short debate as indicated by the Hon. Member, I must add the proviso that I spent some years in opposition when his Party would not accept even one amendment which we proposed. I really think we are going a long way and have been very generous indeed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I simply want to confirm that
there have been considerable negotiations throughout the day.
With respect to the point made by my friend, the Hon.

June 16, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), the understanding is, indeed, that we will complete Bill C-19 at report stage today and tomorrow, assuming that all progresses according to plan, we will complete third reading stage.
Again, to make my point in response to my friend the Parliamentary Secretary, considering the extent of this Bill and the incredible comprehensive changes that will result from its passage, the fact that it has been dealt with in a matter of hours is quite extraordinary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, with respect to Motion No. 95, if the Hon. Member were to seek the unanimous consent of the House to delete the words "-and the need for a special labour adjustment plan" the Government would be amenable to agree to the motion.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with a breaking heart that I will seek the unanimous consent of the House to delete the words "-and the need for a special labour adjustment plan". I appreciate that the Government is ready to accept the first part of the amendment. I cannot win all the wars in one battle. I will accept winning a small battle today and prepare for the next battle on another occasion. I therefore move:

Madam Speaker, during committee consideration of Bill C-18, the Government introduced an amendment to what was then Clause 273 of the Bill but which is now Clause 272. That amendment was portrayed as a technical amendment and one required to facilitate the transfer of the Canadian Transport Commission to the new agency, the National Transportation Agency. We have since become aware that the amendment in question is more than technical in nature.
I have raised this matter with the Parliamentary Secretary, who in turn has discussed with the Government the implications of the amendment. With unanimous consent, I understand the Parliamentary Secretary is willing to move an amendment that will go a long way toward clarifying the situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Wilson (Swift Current-Maple Creek) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   CANADA LABOUR CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
We can no longer allow management and labour to play out these games at the expense of the farm community and, indeed, all Canadians, particularly in times like these. Let no one in the villages, towns and cities of Canada think they are immune to the farm-income crisis. The viability of countless small businesses in the farm service sector depend on the prosperity of the farm community. Indeed, through lost tax revenue and increased farm support programs, a greater burden will fall on other Canadians to pay for the essential and necessary services expected from governments at all levels.
The question then is how much misery, how much cost and how much damage must the rest of us in Canada endure before a settlement must be imposed? Should it be two weeks, five weeks, six weeks? Obviously, there must be a point at which almost all Canadians will agree there has to be a better way. In seeking that better way, I put forward this Bill, not with any illusion that it is perfect or that there may not be better alternatives, but rather to stimulate some much needed debate.
Incredibly, Mr. Speaker, I found this topic has not been debated in this House other than during the usual back-to-work legislation imposed after the damage has been incurred. I believe the matter should be debated in the absence of the emergent conditions and not under the gun in reference to any particular crisis.
The purpose of Bill C-244, in essence, is to declare the handling, storage, transportation and shipping of grain an essential service. It would outlaw strikes and lock-outs in the grain handling and transportation industries and substitute instead a process of binding conciliation. The present mechanism for resolving grain handling disputes works this way: Section 180 of the Canada Labour Code lays out the regulation governing labour disputes in Canada's grain handling and transportation industry. Linder the legislation, no union can strike and no employer can declare a lock-out when the normal collective bargaining process has broken down, unless a number of steps are taken, or at least considered by the federal Department of Labour.
If the process does break down, it is mandatory that the parties inform the Minister of that fact. The Minister may then appoint a conciliation board or a conciliation officer. If the resolution of the dispute is still elusive, the Minister may appoint a conciliation commissioner. The Minister may decide not to appoint a conciliation board or officer, or he may appoint a conciliation board or officer and not appoint a subsequent conciliation commissioner, if the over-all process is not aided by such an appointment.
The Minister may also decide to appoint a mediator without the invitation of the parties involved. In any event, the union attains the right to strike and the employer the right to lockout seven days after either the Minister has notified the parties of his intention to appoint no conciliators in any form, or the Minister has released a copy of the report of the conciliation commissioner to the parties involved in the dispute.
Canada Labour Code
Bill C-244, in brief, would amend the Canada Labour Code by adding a new subsection (3) in Section 180 forbidding strikes or lock-outs in the handling, storage, transportation and shipping of grain. A new Section 171 would make a conciliation report binding on the parties upon the release of the report to them by the Minister. A new Section 164.1.1 would enable either side to request the Minister of Labour to appoint a conciliator. There will obviously be those who oppose this Bill because they will see it as tampering with the right to strike, a right which some see as basic and inalienable, a right which others see as the tyranny of the few. I believe the time has come when this so-called right to strike-

I think we have reached a point where the actions of a few can cause considerable harm and damage to the rest of society. It is clearly time that we reviewed the process.
I am not anti-labour. I am not anti-union. However, I think I have to be against work stoppages which cost all Canadians time and money.

I guess it indicates that the position of the NDP is such that those Members not only need their own time but everyone else's as well. I suggest the Hon. Other critics will say this Bill is dangerous because conciliation may produce something worse than what the parties themselves will eventually conclude. These critics usually quote, erroneously, I believe, the Seaway settlement of 1966 as an example. It is a fact that the Seaway settlement in June 1966 gave a 30 per cent increase to Seaway workers. Because the Seaway was then a Crown corporation and had to have Government appropriations to remain in business, the settlement required Cabinet approval. Cabinet of the day approved the 30 per cent increase, an increase which was unheard of at the time, and the Seaway settlement made any attempt to settle other outstanding disputes between the railways and their non-ops impossible. The result was a disastrous string of fat wage settlements which set off the inflationary spiral in this country throughout the 1970s.
It is important to note that this all stemmed from a Cabinet decision to approve that particular wage settlement. It had nothing whatever to do with the conciliation process we are talking about here today.
Are you indicating, Mr. Speaker, a time problem?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-244 does not change the conciliation process which is already in the Canada Labour Code. It is a process which surely can be no more dangerous tomorrow than it is today. We are not talking about changing the process. We are simply suggesting that it be brought forward. The question therefore is: Should resort be had to the conciliation process later or earlier? I suggest that the time to bring it on is sooner in the process.
It has been suggested that this is not the time to bring on a Bill to amend the Canada Labour Code, that this could be misconstrued in light of current labour difficulties elsewhere. With respect, I can only suggest that at the rate we have stoppages in this country it will be impossible to find the right time.
This Bill was first read in January. It was drawn in the Private Members' lottery in April and it is now being heard. If anything, I believe the current letter carriers' dispute points out the problem that strikes, work stoppages and lock-outs occur far more often in the country than we can tolerate and emphasizes the need for us to find a better way.
I am not saying that this Bill is the best answer, or the only answer. I know only that the present system is fundamentally flawed. Obviously, the issue here is of fundamental importance and requires more than one hour of debate. Frankly, I would welcome a motion during this hour to refer the subject matter to a parliamentary standing committee for further study and recommendation. It may be that the Agriculture Committee would be the appropriate one in the circumstances. What is at stake here is Canada's international reputation as a supplier to the world of high quality wheat.
Many important farm organizations have pointed out the seriousness of the problem and have asked the Government to find a solution. The Keystone Agricultural Producers of Manitoba at its annual meeting of delegates adopted a resolution calling for the handling and transportation of grain to be declared an essential service. The United Grain Growers at its convention last fall called for the Government of Canada
to make Canada's grain handling system an essential service. It also asked the Government to implement a system of binding arbitration with no strikes or lock-outs.
The President of the Western Canadian Wheat Growers recently issued a release in which he states:
We must ensure the system which moves our product does not break down.
Strikes or lock-outs will mean losses, either in reputation or, when stoppages
are long, in sales. In this highly competitive market we can't afford either.
Today, we have a system that is subject to hostage-taking. Unions know that they will be able to play catch-up with large quantities of overtime. There may be times when it suits management to play these games as well. Past history indicates that governments will allow interruptions to last three, four or five weeks until everyone is ready to welcome a government-imposed settlement.
The fact is that strikes and lock-outs have occurred on such a regular basis in Canada that all of the players act in expectation of government intervention. The system is preprogrammed. I suggest it causes the parties to abdicate their responsibility. That being the case, let us have the Government intervene before the damage is done, before the movement of grain is disrupted, before Canada's reputation suffers, and before vital sales are lost. Surely, our society today ought no longer to tolerate a system held ransom to the demands of a few.
We have here a fundamental clash. It is whether the so-called freedom of a small group can be made to override the freedoms of everyone else in the country. Were the damage restricted to the parties alone, one could sit back and let them scrap. The fact is that the misery falls on the backs of all Canadians, primarily on the grain farmer who loses sales and pays demurrage, but also on all Canadians who will wind up having to pay more to help the grain sector survive.
We live in a highly sophisticated society. Our medical people are able to undertake organ transplants. Our scientists are able to put satellites into space. Our high-tech industry has displayed astonishing systems achievements. Yet in the area of the resolution of labour and management problems we are back in the Dark Ages. In the midst of our modern technology and sophistication we see the sad and lamentable spectre of management and labour beating each other on the forehead with rocks until one, or both, fall down.
The issue here is important. I believe it is deserving of more than one hour of debate. There may be better options put forward than Bill C-244. This Bill represents but one approach. There are a great many others. There are in existence specialty courts such as family courts, tax courts, criminal courts, and so on. It may be that we require labour courts. Perhaps we should resort to a two-envelope sort of system wherein the most reasonable of the two competing final positions is chosen. What is important is the recognition of the problem and the potential damage to the Canadian grain farmer and to the nation that flow from work stoppages in the system.
June 16, 1987

Should Members agree with me on this I urge them to pass the Bill or, in the alternative, to refer the subject matter of it to the appropriate parliamentary committee. I do not intend to use my full time because I know other Members want to speak and I am most anxious to hear what they have to say.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   CANADA LABOUR CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all Hon. Members can understand the frustration of the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson) when a strike takes place in an area such as one which deals with the movement of grain. It is a frustrating experience. In some cases it becomes very serious because it affects peoples' lives, their income and their entire future. I can understand why the Hon. Member would propose such an idea even if it is flawed somewhat, both in its premise and in its actual wording.
What I object to in the Bill is that the Hon. Member proposes two things. He says that the Minister shall appoint a conciliation officer, or a board, or a commission, and that the report shall be binding. He then says that no trade union of employees engaged in the handling, storage, transportation or shipping of grain shall declare or authorize a strike anywhere in the country. In other words, no shipper of grain, which includes not only rail but ships, trucks and everything else, involved with the transportation of grain can authorize a strike, and that the report of the conciliation officer shall be binding.
According to the Bill, the Minister would appoint the conciliation officer. So what do we have? For example, we could have a case of a railway about which the Hon. Member is talking and which the Minister can order to cut its expenditures. He could order that CN should decrease its deficit. The Minister could order that after receiving approval from Treasury Board. He is the one who has to make sure that CN meets the projections of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who presents in his Budget the decrease of the deficit of the transporter of grain. Then the Minister would turn around and decide who will be the conciliation officer who will present the binding report. The employees have absolutely nothing to say about this. In other words, the right to strike is removed.
No matter how we look at the situation the right to strike has always been a powerful tool that unions have to force action from governments and employers. So in the case of, say, the Post Office today, or Canadian National today, there are similar situations. There is Treasury Board and the Minister concerned organizing cuts in CN and in Canada Post. Then there are those corporations having to carry through with those cuts in their negotiations with their unions. But it is not the corporation that has decided on the cuts, it is the Minister who has decided upon them. It is Treasury Board that has decided on the cuts. Then along comes this Bill and the Hon. Member says that the Minister will then appoint the person who will decide what happens in the dispute. The Minister cannot appoint someone who is going to suggest the complete opposite to what the Labour Department has announced.
Canada Labour Code
MO)
That is a basic flaw in this Bill. It is particularly flawed in the hands of a government in power such as we have today, the Progressive Conservative Government. The Progressive Conservative Government has a policy of "deficititis". That is what this Government suffers from: a policy of deficititis.
This Government orders transporters of grain to make cuts. It orders the transporters of grain to insist upon double shifts for their employees, to insist upon no wage increases. It issued the same order to Canada Post. Canada Post was told to tell its employees that there would be no wage increase this year; that next year they may get 2 per cent. Also, Canada Post employees have been told that any new employees are subject to a lower wage scale and will never achieve parity with present employees.
This Bill would replace the right to strike with binding conciliation. And who would appoint the conciliator? The Minister concerned. That would be completely unacceptable, Mr. Speaker, under any Government, even a Liberal Government, and particularly so under a Tory Government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   CANADA LABOUR CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise this evening to join in the debate on Bill C-244, the Private Member's Bill of the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson), to amend the Canada Labour Code (grain handling).
During this debate I will speak on behalf of my Party and as one who, along with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), represents the grain handling port of Thunder Bay, or the Lakehead, as it is known. The Port of Thunder Bay is where the last labour stoppage occurred, that having taken place last fall, when the members of BRAC, the grain handlers union, struck the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and, in turn, were locked out by the remainder of the companies with operations at Thunder Bay.
I will be speaking against C-244. 1 think it is a simplistic solution to a very complex problem. It would be a fine world if we could just legislate labour-management relations. However, we cannot just wave the magic wand and have labour and management immediately agree on salaries and working conditions.
While agreements are sometimes achieved in the absence of strike or lock-out actions, the strike weapon must be available to protect workers from the whims of the company. Workers must be able to resort to the age-old right of withdrawal of services, which is what a strike is. It is a collective withdrawal of services arising from dissatisfaction with a given situation.
One of the trade marks of this Government has been its penchant to deal with important and necessary matters in entirely inappropriate ways. When skilful surgery is required, this Government tends to rely on a sledge hammer; when decisive action is required, this Government tends to become mired in confusion and indecision.

June 16, 1987
Canada Labour Code
Consistent with this tendency is Bill C-244, a Bill which proposes to outlaw strikes and lock-outs in the grain handling industry in Canada. While the stated objective of the Bill-the stated objective being to protect Canada's farmers from even more financial hardship-is laudable and can be supported by everyone, the method chosen to meet it is unfair, poorly thought out, and unnecessarily confrontational.
The solution to the massive problems in our farming sector will not be found by creating hardship for other workers. Labour disruption, while unpleasant and extremely difficult for everyone concerned, is a crucial element in the free collective bargaining process.
I have yet to meet a striker who wants to be on strike. Strikers would prefer to be on the job providing their services in exchange for a regular salary. At times, however, the strike proves to be a necessary element in our system of free collective bargaining, a system which has drastically improved the working conditions and standard of living for most Canadians. By interfering in the collective bargaining process, Bill C-244 would do nothing but create a situation in which the parties do not have to bargain seriously, and that is in the best interests of no one.
In the last month, the Seafarers' International Union reached an agreement with the shipping companies operating on the Great Lakes. That agreement was achieved with the assistance of a mediator appointed by the federal Government. Yes, they rattled their swords and talked tough-but they achieved an agreement. The workers did not have to use the strike weapon; the employers did not have to use the lock-out weapon. But those options were available to both sides, thus forcing both to bargain seriously toward an agreement acceptable to both.
It is quite clear that the effect of Bill C-244 has less to do with protecting the interests of the farmer and more to do with union bashing. Since 1917, a span of 70 years, there have been only three work stoppages by grain handlers. Clearly, this is not where the threat to the incomes of farmers comes from. Instead of avoiding the issue by making grain handlers the scapegoat for the problems of our farming sector, government Members should be directing their energies to ensuring that this Government gets serious about treating the farm crisis as the real crisis that it is.
You will well remember the marathon debate that we had in this House this past spring, a debate which brought the country to focus on the plight of the farmers of this country. It was pointed out that while the Government was doing some good things, more was required. Instead of introducing legislation which would make the interests and the welfare of grain handlers secondary to those of other workers, government back-benchers should be encouraging this Government to begin treating all workers fairly and equitably, thus creating a climate in which workers and management can work cooperatively for their mutual benefit.
Not too long ago, we had a situation on the West Coast where the companies locked out their employees. While that lock-out was not restricted to the grain industry, the prairie elevators with terminals in Vancouver participated in that decision. They were part of the Employers' Council which decided to shut down the Port of Vancouver. That was a decision that hurt not only the worker but the farmers who wanted to move their products.
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek might want to spend some time talking with the policy-makers for the pools, the management of the pools about their approach to labour relations. Perhaps he can find out why we no longer have any producers or any grain handlers managing those grain companies. Instead, we have accountants and bookkeepers, and personnel managers. We do not have people who got dirt under their fingernails raising and handling the crop over many years. Therefore, there is not the same kind of understanding about what makes an elevator tick or about what makes good working relationships between management and labour.
In conclusion, I hope the Bill will be rejected in principle by the House. I recognize that it will not come to a vote, but let us try to do something positive. Let us try to ensure that Canadian grain farmers can receive an adequate income, a fair price for their products, and can move those products at a reasonable price and in a way which will keep us competitive in the world. Let us not take it out on grain handlers who are only asking for a decent day's pay for a decent day's work.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in the debate and to support Bill C-244, standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Swift Current- Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson). I think it indicates the importance which western Canadians know must be given to the grain handling system. We in western Canada depend upon a reliable and efficient transportation system to move our grain and oilseeds to market.
As world wheat supplies continue to increase, and as other Governments continue to subsidize wheat exports, Canadian farmers are under increasing pressure to maintain, let alone to expand, their share of the world wheat market. In this very competitive environment, our grain transportation system has proven to be one of Canada's greatest assets.
The system is in a constant state of change. No matter at what part of the system one looks-the railways, the grain terminals, the transfer elevators, or lake transportation-new facilities are added, old facilities are closed; new handling and transportation concepts are introduced and old handling and transportation concepts are ended.
These changes improve Canada's ability to move grain quickly and efficiently from prairie farms to world markets, making the system an important link between producers and world grain markets. Of greatest importance to the changing
June 16, 1987

grain transportation system are the men and women who keep the rolling stock rolling. Many of these people come from farm backgrounds, especially those in the Prairies. They have family and friends who are farmers. They live in communities which are dependent upon the movement of grains and oilseeds to export position as quickly as possible. Their job prospects and their incomes are closely tied to the ability of grain producers to compete in world markets and to move grain to foreign customers. Yet, Canada's grain handling system is beginning to appear unreliable to our foreign customers.
Work stoppages, such as those instituted for Great Lakes shipping, and the increasingly strong threat of strikes or lockouts threaten to undermine the reliability of Canadians to deliver grain.
I should like to quote from a Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association press release dated April 22, 1987. In part it reads:
The Association is supporting the legislation because it does not believe farmers can afford any disruptions in volume movement for their product.
Bill Duke, Chairman of that association, said the following:
Prices for our products are at all-time lows. Our only consolation is volume movement. This situation is likely to continue for some time. We must ensure the system which moves our products does not break down. Strikes or lock-outs will means losses, either in reputation or, when stoppages are long, sales. In this highly competitive market, we can't afford neither.
Under the present mechanism for resolving grain handling disputes, Section 180 of the Canada Labour Code sets out the regulations governing labour disputes in Canada's grain handling and transportation industry. Under the legislation, no union can strike and no employer can declare a lock-out when the normal collective bargaining process has broken down, unless a number of steps are taken or at least considered by the federal Department of Labour.
Section 180 of the Canada Labour Code goes some way toward decreasing the likelihood of a strike or a lock-out, but it does not give security to producers, customers, and western Canadians generally who are dependent upon grain exports.
As other speakers before me have mentioned, and as the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek has said, this topic is too important to cover in one hour of debate in the Chamber. My colleague who introduced this Private Member's Bill mentioned that it may not be the perfect solution. It is certainly not the be-all or end-all, but his purpose in introducing the Bill was to raise the problem and begin discussions because the present system was not working.
The failure of the present system is evidenced by the present rotating mail strikes we are experiencing at the present time, as well as the tie-up in the movement of grain last fall.
In order to ensure that this very important and timely topic gets the full consideration it deserves, I should like to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Fraleigh):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
Canada Labour Code
Bill C-244, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code (grain handling), be not now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in debate on this proposal which attempts to end industrial stoppages in the grain trade. I particularly appreciate the opportunity because I am a Member of Parliament from the Lakehead where we do a great deal of the grain trade.
In the Lakehead, the activities of Lodge 650 of the Brotherhood of Railway, Airline and Steamship Clerks, known familiarly as BRASC, has been very important in the advancement of wages and working conditions of grain handlers. The proposal put forward by the Hon. Member to bring strikes and

June 16, 1987
Canada Labour Code
lock-outs in this industry to an end seems to me to be a misguided effort to achieve certain objectives and specifically to ensure that the costs involved to producers in moving grain are restrained.
The suggestion that strikes or for that matter lock-outs have been used excessively in the grain trade to drive wages to levels which are out of this world and represent an unfair draw on the system seems to me to be quite an unfair suggestion for anyone to make. In Thunder Bay, the reality of which I can speak with some authority is that Lodge 650 of BRASC has been a responsible union representing the interests of its members, workers in the grain trade. In all the years back to the end of the Great War in 1917, there have been only three strikes brought about by the union. That on the very face of it is evidence of a responsible union.
To recognize the fact that the union has been forced to strike occasionally in those years, and on one occasion which was not very long ago, is to recognize that relations that exist in this industry have not always been of the sort that they should be. I think particularly of the fact that several grain companies in Thunder Bay sought two years ago to involve the Government of Canada and Parliament in the industrial relations context, and that was one of the most objectionable features of the situation.
There is nothing gained when there is a breakdown in industrial relations. We want responsible action on the part of the union and on the part of the employer. We want a fair meeting of the two sides at which the union considers what the membership needs and gives due regard to the situation in the industry and the possibility that the industry is able to afford increases in wages or improvements in the benefits package. The union pays due attention to those matters because, after all, if it miscalculates, it can have a disruptive effect on the industry. The union will itself have resources including economists and others to help it put forward a sound case.
On the other side, we expect the employers to give due attention to the situation faced by their workers at the same time as they consider their own potential ability to pay for an improvement in wages or benefits packages. To propose that this proper development in industrial relations should be disrupted in the way put forward by the Hon. Member by outlawing strikes and lock-outs is to impose on workers a peculiar kind of slavery in the workplace that I believe has no place in a free society. After all, the right to withdraw one's services in order to make a point in the mind of one's employer surely must be one of the fundamental rights that workers have always had. To deny the workers the right to stop work and ask their employers to consider their situation, to recognize the fact that wages need to be improved, is surely to depart from the kind of liberal-democratic society we are trying to build and foster in Canada, the kind of society that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of 1982 was surely designed to strengthen.
One might note in passing the lamentable fact that the courts have refused to recognize the right of association and its
consequences as being quite fundamental to society. They have refused to recognize that if the right of association is to mean anything at all, it must include the right to strike, the right to step away from the workplace and tell the employer to consider the situation and improve salaries, benefits and working conditions. To deny that right is surely to subject workers to some kind of slavery.
As someone who grew up on a farm, I would suggest that the imposition of that kind of subjugation in the workplace comes particularly poorly from those who speak for farmers. Obviously farmers work incredibly hard for part of the year and, particularly if they are involved in grain farming, have an opportunity to step away from it, to enjoy curling in the winter or whatever it may be. To demand that the workers at the grain elevators in Thunder Bay, Vancouver, Prince Rupert and Churchill should be subject to the call of their employers without any right to ever break off work in order to consider what they are being subjected to is surely not a principle that anyone would really want to put forward seriously.
I really do believe that the private members of the Conservative caucus who are speaking in support of this proposal are forgetting the principles to which they spoke so strongly in opposition. Very often, they presented themselves as the stoutest defenders of Parliament's rights and of democratic principles. To refuse to recognize the implications of those principles, to try to deny them to workers in Thunder Bay and other cities, seems to be manifestly unfair, particularly when this sort of interference in industrial relations prevails. It is to deny the kind of respect that the former President of Lodge 650 who is now the President of the national union, Frank Mazur, gained over the years from the company and for that matter the kind of respect that he felt for many of the people in the industry with whom he had to deal. They had worked out a good relationship, the kind of relationship that can be evidenced by only two work stoppages in the past two decades. The fact that that only occurred twice was an indication of good industrial relations which, it seems to me, is a real accomplishment.
One of the reasons that I found the lock-out and strike so objectionable that fall was that the employers were very clearly looking to the Government to pull their chestnuts out of the fire, to try to save the situation, to impose something on the worker. That is something we should never do. We should ensure that relations remain between employers and unions at the workplace without any interference of the type which the Member has put forward this afternoon.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the original purpose of a strike was to force the employer to be more reasonable. The original purpose of a lock-out was to force employees to be more reasonable. The difficulty is that while strikes and lock-outs today may hurt the employer or employee a little, they hurt third parties a lot.
June 16, 1987

That is the difficulty with the strikes which have taken place in the grain handling industry. They hurt the farmer who has no way of forcing the people to work or settling their arguments, yet is the one who takes the loss, sometimes permanently. As a matter of fact, as a result of one of the strikes, the prairie farmers lost their pearl barley market and never got that market back. It was lost permanently because of that strike at the West Coast. The producer is the one who is really hurt.
Consequently, in my view in cases like this grain-handling should be considered an essential service. Four or five thousand farmers should not suffer because a handful of people cannot settle their differences. I think compulsory arbitration is the real answer. This is an essential service and there should be neither lock-outs nor strikes. They should be required by law to settle their differences through compulsory arbitration. The farmers are the ones who are hurt and they should not be hurt. People who have nothing to do with the causes of the strike or the lock-out should not be hurt.

Madam Speaker, it is the one and only occasion when my hon. friend was quicker on the draw than I.
In any event, this Bill should not be before the House. Those who appeared before the Transport Committee which studied
June 16, 1987

this Bill, including the Canadian Trucking Association, which is the major player in this legislation, pleaded with the Government not to proceed with this Bill until a new highway safety code was in place, until a national highways board was in place, and until all ten provinces, the territories and the federal Government arrived at a common and reciprocal agreement.
All members in the committee agreed that it was nonsense for a trucker to be required to get licences and operating authorities from 10 provinces and two Territories and from the federal Government if he was going across the line. 1 understand the federal Government vacated that requirement and turned it over to the provinces. That is what will theoretically happen according to Bill C-19.
The Canadian Trucking Association asked to have the national standards and safety provisions agreed upon and implemented by the provinces, the territories and the federal Government. Subsequently, if the Government wants to deregulate the trucking industry, it can do so.
Furthermore, the trucking industry which is comprised of responsible, long-established carriers, made several complaints to the committee in several locations in Canada.
I will never forget one senior officer of a major national trucking company in Canada who told me in Vancouver that he is yet to have a provincial or federal government inspector come to check his mechanics, his garages, his bookkeeping, the hours of work of his drivers or anything else.
He wanted them to ensure they were doing everything properly. More important, he wanted an inspection of the flyby-night operators who can start business under deregulation, simply by conning a banker into giving a loan, then renting some tractors, buying insurance and hiring laid-off drivers at one-third their previous pay. Then they are in business. They have no mechanics or garages. That is what the Government calls "fit, willing and able". But, Madam Speaker, they are unfit. Because they are unfit, the willingness has nothing to do with it. Because they are unfit, they are not able to be on the highways of this country. Look at the record in British Columbia. Last fall the RCMP and the British Columbia Department of Transport, and its Highway Traffic Board, shut down Highway No. 1, the Trans-Canada, near Golden, British Columbia, and checked every truck and one third of those drivers had to be taken off the road.
The Government has no business proceeding with this Bill until all these other matters are in place. There can be no justification for proceeding with this legislation. The amendments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), and myself do nothing more than try to preserve and protect that kind of safeguard in highway transportation. Surely that is not too much to ask. By the way, it is not just the Canadian Trucking Association asking for this. Many others have said: "Look. Do not do it". The last head of the Interstate
Business of the House
Commerce Commission in the United States appeared before our committee as a witness. He said: "For goodness sake, do not make the mistakes we did. Put all these other things in place before you deregulate". The difference between Canada and the United States is that every individual state under its constitution can regulate every trucking company.
Because of this legislation, plus the previous Bill C-18, what an American trucker can do in Canada, a Canadian trucker cannot do in the United States. We can go to the State of New York and Washington, D.C. and talk to Canadian truckers and have them tell us what happens to them when they enter those states. It has nothing to do with the U.S. administration. It has nothing to do with Congress, the Senate, or the House of Representatives. The State of New York places strictures on the Canadian trucker that the Government of Canada cannot do on the U.S. trucker. That is what is going on. Why would the Government be so stupid as to bring in this kind of a Bill now?
Witness after witness, as well as members of the opposition Parties, and some great friends of the Progressive Conservative Party said not to do it yet. They said to put all the other things in place, get all the regulations nailed down, the 10 provinces, the two Territories and the federal Government, and not to bring in Bill C-19 until all those other things are established. Would you believe, Madam Speaker, they will need 200 or 300 more inspectors. The federal Government has agreed to put up a lot of the money, but none of it is in place. There are no inspectors. By the way, one does not pick them up at your average Canada Employment Centre. We do not get those people off the shelf. We have to have someone who knows the difference between an axle, a differential and a diesel engine. Those people cannot be put in place overnight. In fact, that could not happen in less than six months, if we are lucky.
This Bill has no business being called now. It is not the first time the Government had a Bill on the Order Paper for a year, let it die there and put it on again the next year and still did not deal with it until the end of the second year.
Here is an instance where I would agree with the Government. If it takes this Bill off the Order Paper, we will wait another year. That is what was asked for by the Canadian Trucking Association. That is what was asked for in committee by numerous witnesses. This is not the time.
If the Government will not tell us now that it will not proclaim this Bill until all those things I have mentioned are in place, then we have no alternative but to oppose the Bill. If it holds off proclamation until all those other things are in place, the Government might have less trouble tonight and tomorrow.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the amendments under debate at this particular moment in time have to do with Clause 8. There are three separate motions, as I read it, under debate. This is a Government which purports to be working with the provincial Governments, a Government which purports to be working with the transportation industry. This is from a Government that says it will consult and that it has consulted. It states in Clause 8 that the provincial transport board in each province "may" issue a licence. That is the first part of Clause 8.
It must be kept in mind that the provincial Departments of Transport have said no to this Bill as it stands without a national safety code included. The clause does not state that it can issue a licence, or that the Government will not object if it does issue a licence but that it "may" issue a licence. In fact, this is the federal Government speaking to the provincial Governments which have not agreed to this legislation unless a safety code is put in place.
Clause 8(2) states that the provincial transport board in a province "shall" issue a licence. In effect, this is from the federal Government which is passing a law affecting the provincial Governments when the provincial Governments have said no to the Bill unless a safety code is brought in.
If that were not bad enough we must contend with subclause (3) of Clause 8. It is stated in that clause that the provincial transport board is "authorized" to hold a public hearing. I ask Hon. Members to imagine the Government saying to a provincial transport board: "Yes, you can hold a public hearing". It then states that the board shall not hold a public hearing with respect to an application for a licence referred to in subclause (2). This is legislation put forward by the federal Government which does not have the agreement of the provincial Governments to bring in such regulations. It goes so far as to say that the board, that is, the provincial transport board, shall not hold a public hearing. This is from a Government which says: "We consult. We agree with what the provinces say".
June 16, 1987

If that were not bad enough, there is Subclause (4) of Clause 8 to contend with. That subclause states that the provincial transport board is not required to issue a licence referred to in subclause (2). This is again from the federal Government which is telling a provincial board what it has to do when it does not have the agreement of the provincial governments.
Then in Subclause (5) it is stated that a provincial transport board "shall" and in Subclause (6) it states that the provincial transport board "may not".
What is wrong with this Bill? It is obvious what is wrong with it. It is a gigantic intrusion into provincial jurisdiction without the approval of provincial boards.
I could not care less if it were without the approval of the provincial Governments but with the approval of the people affected in the provinces. Here we have the Government pointing out that there shall not be public hearings, that a province may, a province shall, a province ought to. The Government has done this without the approval of the provincial Governments, without the input of local truckers or the input of the local people who have to pay for their services.
In effect, this is a Bill which will say to poor Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, P.E.I. and British Columbia-the extremities of the country: "You will no longer have the control that you had over who delivers goods and services in your area of the country. You are going to accept what we say. We even lay down for you what your provincial boards can and cannot do. We will not stop there. We will say whether you can have public hearings or not".
That is an outrageous intrusion not only into provincial jurisdiction but into the jurisdiction of the public. The jurisdiction of the public deals with having a say over what its transportation network will be like, whether or not it will have to pay more for the transportation of its goods, whether or not there will be one trucker left in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or British Columbia.
When there are large trucking outfits that can travel the country it is obvious that under this legislation they will be controlled by federal jurisdiction which is imposed at the provincial level. Basically, I would have to say that with the three amendments that are put forward by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) the Government of Canada is surpassing the bounds of good judgment when it comes to relations with the provinces and relations with the people who live in those provinces.
The board referred to in Clause 8 is normally referred to in most provinces as a public utilities board. There are different names for it in different provinces. A trucker will go in and apply to that board for a licence. Sometimes within provinces the board has already issued licences to companies that are established in that area, or to companies which normally provide service in that area.
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
The boards also work with the Departments of Finance to regulate the movement of trucks. That is what this board referred to in this particular clause in each province does. These boards even make regulations pertaining to a trucker buying gasoline.
A trucker cannot fill up his truck with gasoline in the State of Maine and go through four or five provinces without paying sales tax on the gasoline in that truck. That is what the weigh scale stations are for. We often wonder what they are for. They are not just to weigh the commodities in the trucks. They are there to measure the amount of gasoline that is in a truck's tank. The people at the weigh station ask the truckers where they are going in their particular province. If the trucker says: "We are going on this particular road for x-number of miles and we are not going to buy any gas or oil for the truck", then the department in the particular province will compute the amount of tax one would have to pay if one had purchased one's fuel in that particular province. Every trucking company knows about that.
The reason this is done is that it might be possible to find some trucks with a couple 100-gallon tanks on either side and the trucker has gassed up in the State of Maine. In Maine we do not have to pay the taxes that we pay at the provincial and federal levels in Canada. The price of gasoline is much cheaper since the oil has been exported by Canada to the United States to be refined.
In this clause the federal Government makes a massive intrusion into provincial jurisdiction. What we strongly object to is that it is without the approval of the provincial government and without the adoption of a national safety code. The federal Government says: "No public hearings. You will not have a say, general public, in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or British Columbia. It is the Government of Canada. Here is what we are dishing out. Take it whether you like it or not".

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the points raised by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and the Hon. Member for Gander- Twillingate (Mr. Baker).
The whole question of motor vehicle transport in Canada has always been a complex one, given the federal-provincial jurisdictional split. Over the years, as our society has become more sophisticated, motor vehicle transport has become increasingly complicated.
All of the studies done over the years indicated the need for a federal-provincial agreement in this area. I am referring here to studies done by the Economic Council of Canada going back to 1978, interdepartmental studies conducted under the auspices of the previous Government, as well as the many studies conducted by the provinces.

June 16, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
In February of 1985 we had a memorandum of understanding signed by the federal Government and the provinces as to how this matter should be resolved. It was an 11-government agreement. All parties agreed that we had to get our act together.
In the light of that, I cannot understand the remarks of my hon. friend, the Member for Gander-Twillingate. Bill C-19 flows from that 11-government agreement.
While we have always had safety guidelines in place, they have been diverse and diffuse. Again in this area all of the 11 Governments came together, with a memorandum of understanding on a national safety code being signed in March of this year. There was unanimous agreement that when Bill C-19 comes into force on January 1, 1988, over 50 per cent of that national safety code will be in place-and that, in itself, is an enormous improvement over the existing situation. There is agreement that the balance will come into effect by January 1, 1990.
It is in that context that Hon. Members should be considering Bill C-19. To be quite frank, I am at a loss to understand some of the points raised.
It is true that the Canadian Truckers' Association, the driving force behind the unanimous agreement, has expressed some doubts with respect to the national safety code. It is the view of that association that it may be that it would be best to have the entire code go into effect at the same time.
However, the Government, with the concurrence of the committee, believes that the wiser course would be to put it into place as it is ready. It can always be added to or amended over the course of time.
This Government has lived up to its commitment to make safety the number one priority. Hon. Members will be aware that we now have a new Aeronautics Act and a new Canada Shipping Act. As well, we now have in place regulations governing the transport of dangerous goods. In 1984, there were 1,030 safety inspectors in place. Today, we have 1,156, and there will be more added as time goes on.
We are in the process of drafting a new rail safety Act. We have the response to the Foisy report. We are drafting a new transportation accident investigation board Act. As well, the new National Trucking Safety Code will be 50 per cent in force on the proclamation of Bill C-19, with the rest coming into force within a few months following its proclamation.
The concerns with respect to safety are misplaced. They got into problems in the U.S. because they chose to deregulate everything, everywhere, and all at once, all in the absence of having any agreements in respect of safety in place. That is not the case in Canada. We are not doing that at all.

Madam Speaker, as the Member of Parliament for Winnipeg North, Winnipeg being a city to which transportation, whether it be by air, by rail, or truck, is of utmost importance, I could not let this debate come to a close without saying a few words.
In bringing forth this Bill, we see a Government so blinded by its ideology that it ignores the warnings and the questions raised by every sector of the community. The trucking industry has raised serious objection to this Bill. It has urged that deregulation not be proceeded with until a number of very important questions have been answered.
The Province of Manitoba itself has raised some major concerns in respect of Bill C-19.
Deregulation in the trucking sector, as deregulation for the railways or the airlines, may bring benefits to the major centres of this country, but not to the regions. While it may result in cheaper rates and better service in the Quebec City-Windsor axis, while it may result in benefits in terms of the traffic between Calgary and Edmonton, it will do nothing for the northern communities of this country, the farming communities, the cities off the mainstream, such as Lethbridge, all of which will suffer very seriously as a result of this mania for deregulation, regardless of its consequences.
The Parliamentary Secretary has implied that all the provinces have agreed to the provisions of Bill C-19. I have here a letter from the Manitoba Minister for Highways and Transportation analysing the defects in the Bill and raising some very serious questions about it, questions which were ignored by the Government in bringing forth Bill C-19.
The letter is addressed to the federal Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and is dated August 8, 1986.
I shall take a moment to go over some of the questions raised in the letter. Before doing so, let me again point out to the Parliamentary Secretary that not one of the questions raised by the Minister of Highways and Transportation for the
June 16, 1987

Province of Manitoba has been answered by the Government or dealt with in the Bill. As well, he knows very well that the provincial and national trucking associations have raised serious objection to this Bill, for a variety of reasons, none of which have been satisfied.
I remind the Hon. Member that the trucking companies in Manitoba headquartered around Steinbach are among those who have raised very serious objection to this Bill. These are people from whom, in my wildest expectations, I would never expect a vote for the New Democratic Party.
Let me just put on record some of the observations of the Manitoba Minister of Highways and Transportation. In his letter he wrote:
-the new National Safety Code and Fitness Entry Test are not adequate on their own to ensure an appropriate level of highway safety-
The Parliamentary Secretary said that safety would be ensured, but this was from a Government which cut back on the number of public servants in every area. We do not have the same number of people to inspect trucks to ensure that they are structurally sound or to ensure that truck drivers, in their need to meet competition, do not drive 18 hours or 20 hours at a stretch. It is this situation in the United States which has led to many accidents.
Also the Minister wrote:
-small and remote communities and small shippers will not receive adequate service and will be subject to excessive price discrimination, without intervention-
If we let anybody and everybody who has a truck compete for some of the rural communities in the Interlake part of Manitoba or in The Pas-Flin Flon-Thompson area represented by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), it will not be very long before prices are so competitive that some of them will go out of business and we will have no regular, assured service.
Also the Minister wrote:
-American trucking giants are likely to dominate Canadian and transborder trucking markets to the detriment of our national interest-
Canadian trucking companies, which did relatively well in getting business in the United States when it deregulated, now realize that the American companies have a market 10 times the size of the Canadian market and are being forced, because of deregulation in the U.S., to operate under cut-throat competition. They would be very happy to move into the Canadian market. They are so much bigger than Canadian trucking companies that our companies are frightened, with justification, that they will be driven out of business.
Then the Minister indicated:
-cutthroat competition will result in instability in the trucking industry and undue exploitation of trucking employees.
The reasons for the Minister saying that are obvious. That is precisely what will happen if we have free, unfettered competition.
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
With the desire to stay in business, prices will be cut, safety will be ignored, and the hours which truckers drive without stopping will be lengthened, and we will have the inevitable results-more and more accidents.
I should like to refer to some of the other concerns expressed by the Manitoba Minister, none of which were answered in the Bill.
He wrote that the following be considered:
-all shippers, particularly small shippers and those located in small and remote communities of Canada, receive adequate service at rates that are not excessively discriminatory-
Obviously the Minister is worried about small communities. If, in order to keep some of the business, trucking companies must cut their prices between main centres in Canada or between main centres in Canada and the United States, obviously they will make up their losses in that very competitive market by increasing prices or cutting services to smaller remote communities. He also wrote:
-the Canadian trucking industry is sufficiently stable and viable.
That needs to be assured before we proceed with deregulation. He went on to say:
-the Canadian trucking industry is in a position to compete on even terms with foreign carriers-
That should have been assured before we proceeded with deregulation. He continued by indicating that a minimum level of Canadian control of the trucking capacity in Canada should be assured.
We have had thousands of takeovers, and there will be increasing take-overs by American companies of Canadian trucking companies. Canadian sovereignty will be lessened. Then the Minister suggested that we needed the following:
-an appropriate balance of trade in trucking services with foreign nations-
We are sitting a few miles from a country which has a population 10 times the size of Canada's. He also indicated that appropriate working conditions and levels of remuneration for those employed in trucking and an appropriate level of highway safety in Canada must be assured.
I know that our time is limited, but I should like to say that the Bill does not meet any of the necessary conditions mentioned by the Manitoba Minister of Highways and Transportation before we proceeded with it. This is why we are opposing the amendment.

Madam Speaker, I would like to say a word or two. I probably will not say it as well as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Thacker) would have.
I know a little about the trucking industry, particularly in the Province of Alberta. I want to assure the Hon. Member who just spoke and the rest of the House that our truckers are not violently opposed to the Bill. As a matter of fact, Alberta truckers support the Bill.
Alberta truckers are probably the most knowledgeable of freedom to move of any truckers in the country, because for a number of years Alberta truckers have been virtually operating under freedom to move. They have one of the finest trucking associations in the country, bar none.
When people stand up and say that all these terrible things will happen, I do not know what they are talking about. We are not under a freedom to move system yet. All the things about which they are talking have happened under a regulated system, not under a deregulated system. Besides, this Party and this Government are not out for holus-bolus deregulation. We do not believe in regulating everybody's lives; of course we do not. That is part of the NDP philosophy. We believe in the Government reflecting the thinking of the people in its legislation and in its administration.
I want to talk for a few moments about the United States taking over all our trucking. For a number of years, U.S. trucks have been able to move into Alberta and Alberta trucks have been able to move into the United States. There has been free movement back and forth. It has not resulted in the Americans taking over our trucking, not at all. It has resulted in benefits for the U.S.A. and benefits for Canada, benefits for Alberta. It has been a mutually beneficial thing, because when Alberta truckers go into the United States, they respect its laws, and American truckers respect our laws when they come into Alberta or elsewhere in Canada.
They are truckers, and I want to say a word or two about truckers; I have had a lot to do with them. They are not illiterate and they are not immature. They are a mature group of people. There might be an odd few who will try to work 20 or 24 hours, as the Hon. Member just mentioned, and there
might be the odd few who will take pills to try to stay awake, but they are the exception. That type of exception may take place under any system. However, the vast majority of truckers in Canada are sound, mature, able, and efficient operators. I say that with double strength because I know what I am talking about. They are not out to beat the consumers, they are out to give a service and to make an honest living. I think we should recognize that our truckers are excellent people.
People are saying that we will suddenly see an era without safety. What have our Departments of Highways and our motor transport boards been doing for the last 25 or 30 years? They have been building up a safety system in every province. Now trucks are operating from British Columbia to Montreal, from Edmonton to Halifax, going through every province and observing the rules of every province. It is very difficult for truckers to operate across Canada because every one must get the consent of each motor vehicle transport board to move through the province. It is like 10 Balkan states. This legislation will enable us to become a united nation. I hope the day will come very soon as we advance with this type of legislation that someone with a licence in Alberta who is qualified and has the proper insurance will be able to travel any place in Canada as a nation without having to stop in every province to get a permit.
A few years ago, the situation was even worse. Some Alberta truckers wanted to bring frozen beef to Montreal. The only way they could do that was to go through the United States because the licence fees for an Alberta truck to go through Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and then into Quebec were so high. These truckers had to get a permit from every province. When there are interveners, these permits can cost as much as $20,000 or $25,000 and sometimes even more than that, depending on how many accountants and lawyers are required, how much travelling must be done and how many people oppose it. It is done on the basis of convenience and necessity.
Under the old system, one trucker would get a monopoly and then add truck after truck so that no one else could get into the market. There could be no competition. That is still evident in some places in Canada. We want competition but we do not want monopolies. By working with the laws in this Bill and in Bill C-18, we will be able to get our Canadian truckers to operate across the nation. They will become a viable competitor of the railways and of the airlines and that is the way it should be.
I recall a few years ago when the railways went on strike, they said that truckers could not haul cars. Well, the truckers soon showed them. They got their lowboys out and hauled cars across the nation. They did it cheaper than the railways ever did. Truckers are a viable competitor and we want every mode of transport to have a chance to contribute to the country.
June 16, 1987

There are some things that the trains can do best. There are some things that truckers can do best. There are some things that the airlines can do best. There are some things that the pipelines can do best. Some things can even go by ship around the country and have cheaper and better service. However, every mode should have the opportunity to compete fairly and that is what we are aiming at.
Before we began to deal with freedom to move, there were at least 18 or 20 trucks in the United States to every truck in Alberta. Now it has gone the other way. Under freedom to move, it is almost one for one. Our truckers have healthy businesses in the United States and they employ Canadians.
The trucking industry will thrive under this legislation. It will give truckers the first chance they have had for years to compete ably. I am not afraid at all of American trucks taking over our trucking industry. As a matter of fact, I asked an American who appeared before our committee if he was afraid of the Canadian trucks taking over the American trucks and he said that maybe I had something there. Our truckers are just as wise, knowledgeable and efficient and perhaps even more so than any American trucker. Our truckers are one fine group and I am not afraid at all that they cannot compete ably and provide a service to Canada.
I support this Bill. What about all these wild dreams about the roads becoming unsafe? The roads being built today are built well with good gradients, good sight distances, good curves and they will improve. They will get better and better. We have excellent engineers in Canada and our truckers will be able to operate ably because they will be well trained.
We will not stop training truckers and we will not stop checking motor vehicles because we are changing the system. We will do it more so. It will be in the truckers' best interests to keep their vehicles roadworthy and to give their drivers proper wages and hours of work. In that way, they will make a contribution to Canada that they have never been able to make before, a contribution they have been denied the right to make. I congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary for sponsoring this Bill and I think it will mean great things for Canada.
