speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the rhetoric of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). No one would oppose much of what he had to say. Everyone supports a system that would bring some kind of redress to the Balkanization of the permit system in Canada, but what the Hon. Member and the Government have not addressed is the point raised by my colleague from Regina and my friend from Thunder Bay.
I believe we must look pretty carefully at what this Bill really means. The Hon. Member has said that this kind of competition will be good, but anyone who has taken a close look at the implications of what happened in Australia and various places in the United States like California as a result of deregulation would scratch his head and wonder why the
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
Government did not bring in the safety criteria and the regulations first so that truckers knew what they would get.
As I said earlier this evening, the Members on the government side were always the ones who went after the Liberals whenever they brought in a Bill that had a clause like Clause 8 which provided that the Governor in Council could make all the regulations after the Bill is passed. It provides for Trojan Horse regulatory powers. The Hon. Member for Bow River has always fought against that in the House but he seems to be overlooking it this evening.
This Bill will lead to competition that will lead to monopolies. I would like to put a few facts on the record indicating what this really means for small truckers from Skeena, Newfoundland, northern Ontario and some of the regions where small routes have been developed over time. In those areas, truckers move a little bit of this to there and another commodity over there and back-haul something else. They just manage to find themselves a niche and can keep one, two or ten trucks on the road.
The Hon. Member speaks of fit, willing and able. We know what the definition of that is in the Bill. Anyone who can get a bank or credit union to give him the financing to get a couple of tractors, some insurance and a couple of drivers will be considered under this legislation to be fit, willing and able.
Let us look at the Canadian trucking sector. Trucking accounts for 50 per cent of all the transportation revenue in Canada. That amounted to about $5 billion last year, not including revenue raised by fleets owned by companies that do their own hauling. Some very substantial hauling is done by those fleets. For example, earlier this evening we were talking about a large hauler like Canadian Tire and what happens when Canadian Tire takes a large amount of product from Toronto.
Let us say they take it to Terrace or Gander, Newfoundland, and drop it off where historically a small regional trucking operator would be hauling various commodities in the province and perhaps beyond the province into another region. They cannot possibly compete when Canadian Tire is getting from the consumer the cost of trucking. They simply pay the driver and pay for the rubber, the diesel, the gas and so on, for an empty back-haul. That opens a whole new era of trucking in Canada for such corporations.
Let us take a look at the safety questions. Important evidence was put before the Transport Committee which was not listened to by the government side. In the event of an accident involving a car and a truck, the driver of the car is 40 times more likely to be killed. Twelve Canadians a day are dying right now on our highways. Competition at the expense of safety was blamed for a 40 per cent increase in accidents in California after deregulation there in 1980. It is exactly that kind of competition which the Canadian industry is now alarmed about.

June 16, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
In British Columbia just a few months ago there was a landmark coroner's inquest into brakes and safety matters with regard to large tractor trailer operations. The loosening of front axle brakes on tractor trailers has been proliferating, particularly in British Columbia. Evidence was given by the manager of fleet safety for the Insurance Corporation of B.C. Mr. Fergus Savage told the inquest that 60 per cent of the heavy trucks on B.C. highways are operating without those brakes "the highest per centage in Canada", and that most drivers wrongly believe that they are better off without them. The evidence he gave included a report by NBC in the United States which attributed thousands of road fatalities on U.S. highways to the lack of such brakes on heavy trucks.
The Government says that this is only to break down the Balkanization of the permit system. That seems to be its selling line for this legislation. The fact is that the key issue, which is safety on the highways and safety of the truckers, has not been addressed.
Some of the other evidence in relation to Bill C-19 is very worthy of consideration. Predation should have been more directly addressed in Clause 8. It includes the entire sequence of issuance of licences, public hearings, how to file objections, implementation, limitations and regulation. Predation is clearly an issue which the Government has not fully thought through. If it has, it has simply opted in favour of the very large Canadian trucking operators which will pick up a lot of the smaller rural forward and back-haul routes.
After 30 years of deregulation in Australia three trucker/forwarders control 70 per cent of the interstate transportation market-place. In the United States the degree of concentration in the LTL industry since 1980 has surprised everybody. The fact is that not one new general freight carrier has been able to enter the market-place since U.S. deregulation.
Government Members get up and say that this will create a whole new era, that all kinds of new corporations will be formed, there will be all kinds of new profit, that prices will come down, consumers will be better served, and truckers will be free to haul beef from Alberta to Toronto without having to go through the U.S. and so on. The fact is that that which happened in California which has roughly the same population as Canada and roughly the same amount of traffic tonnage movement was quite different.
There are no new entrants into the market-place. There is no long-term competitive downward pricing for the movement of commodity which is supposed to be to the benefit of consumers. Instead new monopolies which were not there in the past have been created. The monopoly structures get rid of the independent truckers which have always been in the marketplace, the small guy, the Ma and Pa operations with one, two, five or ten trucks. Those are the ones which will disappear and there will be massive expansion of the big ones such as Canadian Freightways.
Another thing which should have been looked at more carefully in Clause 8 which the Government likes to skate around is that which has happened in relation to U.S. carriers coming into the Canadian market. The largest U.S. carrier that has been in the Canadian market the longest, Canadian Freightways, while dominant in the western Canadian general freight market, has certainly not been a cut-rate operator. Indeed, Canadian Freightways have been exemplary in creating a separate Canadian identity.
The trouble is that few, if any, of the more recent U.S. entrants have shown similar tendencies. Rather, they seem to regard a few sectors of the Canadian market as nothing more than convenient extensions of their U.S. operations where marketing policies are determined from outside Canada and possibly beyond the purview of BCP in any practical sense.
Let us take a look at what has happened with those carriers. A submission to the standing committee in 1985 relied in large part on the Boucher study which claimed that the big U.S. carriers are complementary to Canadian carriers and no threat at all to domestic carriers in short-haul international LTL or domestically. Approximately two months before BCP's presentation to the standing committee one of the largest U.S. general freight carriers, Yellow Freight, sought and obtained multipoint operating authority throughout Quebec. Two months later another of the U.S. mega carriers, Roadway, obtained broad-based authority throughout Ontario. Now all three U.S. continental giants have broad-based authority in the key Canadian markets.
What has the Government done? It has been in office since 1984. There has been no movement on safety and no movement to deal with the penetration of U.S. carriers. The Member for Bow River says that to haul Alberta beef from Alberta to Ontario we have to go through the U.S. and meet all of their interstate criteria. This is not the way to deal with the Balkanization of permits. No Member of this House should knowingly vote for this Bill telling truckers that that is what it is for. We should be dealing with a different kind of permiting system and with safety first.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to deal with the amendments which have been introduced by my colleagues which go directly to the root of this legislation, Bill C-19, which has been vigorously opposed by the truckers' associations. It is surprising that the Government has gone ahead to deal with such legislation while those concerned are so vehemently opposed to it.
I will quote representations made before the standing committee by the Ontario Trucking Association which to me, more than any other, echo the concerns of truckers across Canada and identify the three principal areas of concern, those being, first, that all of the essential ingredients for implementing and enforcing a uniform national safety code will not be in place by the proposed date of regulatory change, second, that there are no measures at hand in the Bill to combat unsafe or predatory pricing and, third, that Canadian carriers will be at
June 16, 1987

a significant competitive disadvantage with U.S. carriers because of more onerous taxation and social policies.
Let me first deal briefly with the issue of the uneven playing field with which Canadian truckers have to contend and which places them at a significant competitive disadvantage to their American counterparts. I would like to quote from a letter sent by the Canadian Trucking Association to members of the standing committee. I heard my colleagues who spoke earlier, particularly the very important member of the standing committee, the very venerable Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). Indeed, he knows a lot about the trucking industry and has a very distinguished career in the Province of Alberta dealing with transportation matters. Therefore, he should be aware of the feeling of the Canadian Trucking Association.
I am sure that he must have received this letter. I was a little surprised by his presentation and I just want to refresh his memory by quoting the letter from the Canadian Trucking Association that was sent to all members of the standing committee. It states: "It is not simply a question of whether U.S. truckers will have a long-term cash flow advantage over Canadian truckers. If the disparity is as great as it appears, the Canadian truckers who are serious about long-term participation in serving an integrated continental transportation market-place will increasingly be persuaded to relocate their international operations in the United States, operating back into this country using U.S. equipment and U.S. employees".
It goes on to state: "The implication of that scenario goes far beyond the immediate interests of truckers".
Yet the Government has failed to move. Numerous representations to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) only met with disinterest. One hopes that when the Minister tables his long awaited White Paper on taxation Thursday night he will address the concerns of the trucking industry, particularly with regard to the issue of compensation for loss of value of operating authority.
I am a little skeptical of the desire of the Government to move so quickly with Bill C-19. It was even asking that we deal not only with report stage, but third reading tonight. Is that because on Thursday night the Minister of Finance will forget the Canadian truckers? Is it because government Members, the Parliamentary Secretary and the Deputy Government House Leader know something we on this side of the House do not know and want to be sure that this legislation is disposed of before the truckers realize Friday morning that the Minister of Finance has forgotten them, thereby putting them in deep trouble in the face of competition from the American truckers?
The Parliamentary Secretary is shaking his head and I suspect that he is saying that he does not know. I hope I am wrong and that indeed the Minister of Finance will not forget the Canadian truckers Thursday night.
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
At any rate, I support the amendments that have been moved by my colleagues from the New Democratic Party and hope that these amendments are accepted because at least they will improve very bad legislation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will not spend much time but since one of the motions is in my name, I feel I should contribute to the discussion.
The motions in the name of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and myself refer to fundamental matters in Bill C-19 and, as indicated by the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), attempt to make a bad Bill better.
We have great concerns about the direction in which the country is heading in terms of truck transportation. We believe that while there needs to be a re-examination of regulation and the manner in which we require motor carriers to operate, the Government has gone too far too fast with this legislation. The whole question of safety has not been addressed to the extent we believe appropriate.
I want to read into the record a letter from the Canadian Trucking Association that was sent to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). It is dated June 2, 1987, and is a follow-up to their appearance before the Standing Committee on Transport which was charged with the responsibility of reviewing Bill C-19.
The letter states:
Re: Safety of Commercial Highway Vehicles
During the hearings before the Standing Committee on Transport on Bill C-19 where CTA stressed its concern over highway safety implications of deregulation, we were accused by shippers of having raised a "phoney" issue on grounds that there was no evidence of a connection between motor carrier deregulation and safety deterioration from the U.S. experience. Shippers are still saying that. Indeed, your own departmental advisers appear to have adopted much the same approach.
On the basis that the debate over whether we are going to deregulate is now over, I would like to take this opportunity to hopefully set the record straight based on comprehensive documentation that has come out of the United States relating to the commercial vehicle safety problem.
The attached booklet on highway safety and the relationship with deregulation was prepared on behalf of the Coalition for Sound General Freight Trucking which I take it is a coalition of U.S. trucking associations including American Trucking Associations. The point here is that these U.S. trucking interests are not raising the connection between safety and deregulation for the purpose of turning the clock back. There would be no point in that and the same holds true here.
An objective overview of the attached material can lead to only one conclusion; namely, that there has been a marked deterioration in highway safety for particular segments of the U.S. trucking industry in recent years and the position continues to deteriorate despite serious attempts to introduce more effective highway safety enforcement.
We have a huge job to be done in Canada on safety and time is of the essence, as we tried to tell the Committee.
Due to the erosion of the regulatory process in recent years, the Canadian trucking industry has come under much the same pressure as its U.S. counterpart and the position is anything but satisfactory as things stand. It can only get worse. In that regard, you may be aware that the Quebec Department of Transport recently introduced a comprehensive on-highway enforcement crackdown on highways leading into Montreal and Quebec City. The initial

June 16, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
results from that exercise show that well over 50 per cent of vehicles inspected were in violation of either safety or licensing requirements.
May I add that this is under a regulated system. The letter continues:
More and more Canadian carriers operating in the U.S. are now being picked up for serious safety violations there.
CTA and its provincial affiliates are coming under pressure from individual carriers who are not at all happy with the position we have taken on safety. The fact is that there are established fleets operating on a regular basis that push their drivers beyond 20 hours in a shift. If one carrier does it, everyone has to do it to remain competitive. It is just as simple as that.
In that regard, industry executives who attended the recent CCMTA Safety Code meetings remain concerned over the seeming lack of urgency in getting on with implementation and enforcement of key elements of the National Safety Code.
Extra provincial hours of service regulation is a fiasco as things stand and will seemingly remain so until about 1990. In addition there may be a jurisdictional problem which CTA raised the best part of two years ago concerning private fleets and the issue has still not been addressed as far as we know. Last week at a CTA Conference and Annual Meeting, grave concerns were raised about the delay in getting on with comprehensive enforcement of essential elements of the Safety Code. Clearly the most critical aspect is hours of service followed closely by vehicle inspection, all requiring an effective enforcement regime.
Concerns are heightened due to the exemptions that CCMTA proposes to incorporate into any new hours of service regime.
It is difficult enough to obtain reliable records on hours of service without riddling the regime with loopholes and exemptions. These should be kept to a minimum otherwise it makes effective enforcement virtually impossible.
There is only one way to address the fundamental problems and that is through meaningful and ongoing safety enforcement that treats everyone equally. Having 50 per cent of a paper regime in place by the beginning of deregulation in 1988 will do very little to improve things.
What is required now is hands-on federal involvement in the process of getting the Safety Code in place by assisting the handful of dedicated provincial officials who have taken on this responsibility. Federal funding alone will not do the job.
It is signed by A. K. Maclaren, Vice President, Government Relations, of the Canadian Trucking Association.
I think its letter to the Minister expresses very clearly the concerns of the industry. I know my time is running out, but I just want to say to Members of the House that we are very concerned about safety and about the impact of this Bill regardless of our philosophical problems. We are going ahead much too fast and the industry and the provinces need the time to put the mechanisms in place to ensure our highways will be safe.

Motion No. 4.
That Bill C-19, be amended in Clause 9 by adding immediately after line 16
at page 6 the following:
"(/) to prevent unfair pricing practices by an extra-provincial truck undertaking;".
He said: Madam Speaker, very briefly, I would like to say that unfair pricing practices are a matter of serious concern to
June 16, 1987

the trucking industry in Canada. Obviously, in an open market where competition is the name of the game, there will be a tendency for shippers to seek out the lowest possible rates. That is of course one of the great benefits of deregulation-

We must be very careful, indeed, because testimony before the California Public Utilities Commission in February, 1987, provides significant insight into the dangers of unfettered price competition. Volume discounts and rate reductions have become the order of the day in California. Several carriers have not had any increase at all in their rate levels since 1980. Moreover, a price floor has never been achieved in California. Some carriers have always been willing to cut their rates further to get a shipment. Indeed, transportation is a perishable product and a missed load could never be recaptured. That seems to be the prevailing philosophy in California and I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that it could be the prevailing philosophy in Canada after deregulation of the transport industry takes place.

We feel that the acceptance of Bill C-19 as it now exists would seriously damage the highway transportation industry in Canada. Major American carriers will be among those who will apply for the more readily available licences. According to Canadian industry representatives, foreign take-overs of Canadian highway carriers will multiply over the next five years. Since 1981, the operating costs in Canada have increased by 28 per cent, due mainly to the high tax on fuel and the tremendous costs of liability insurance. Over the same period, the traffic has increased by only 5 per cent. As a net result, the profit margin is now down to 3 per cent, one of the lowest since World War II.
Well, major American firms, sometimes with individual gross sales higher than those of the whole Canadian industry, could enter the Canadian market, lower their rates, offering predatory rates, absorbing losses for a couple of years and finally purchasing completely exhausted Canadian highway carriers.
That is the risk of introducing such fitness criteria at a time when the Canadian industry is operating with a 3 per cent profit margin and when the very survival of the Canadian trucking industry is at stake.
Our major concern is that the Combines Investigation Act would be inadequate to prevent this kind of competition.

In all the history of the provisions, which date back to the early 1950s, only six cases have come to the courts. Only one conviction has been obtained. That was for goods given away in large quantities for a period of one year. The reasons for such an ineffectiveness are clear. Predatory pricing is a criminal versus a civil offence under the Competition Act. All elements of the offence must be satisfied by the criminal standard of proof which is proof beyond a reasonable doubt,
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
and all criminal law defences are available, including now the Charter of Rights.
The pricing inquiry into Canadian newspapers is a good example of how illusory our Competition Act could be. Marshalling sufficient evidence to meet the criminal standards of proof is very difficult and is the reason most often cited by the Director of Combines for discontinuing inquiries. The courts have said that the evidence must be strong in order to convince them to intervene and convict. As Mr. Moore in his book, How Much Price Competition!, said: "The battle is likely to be over before the case is completed".

It is to remedy these major shortcomings that we have moved motion No. 4, which would allow the Governor in Council, following consultation with the government of each province, to make regulations in order, and I quote:
"to prevent unfair pricing practices by an extra-provincial truck undertaking;"
I hope, therefore, that my colleagues in the House will accept this motion which I feel is essential to reinforce Bill C-19 as well as the Canada Competition Act.

Motion No. 7 A
That Bill C-19, be amended in Clause 33 by striking out lines 37 to 40 at
page 13 and substituting the following therefor:
"33.(1) This Act except this section and sections 3 and 9 shall come into force on a date prescribed by the Governor in Council after the implementation of regulations respecting the safe operation of extraprovincial bus undertakings or extra-provincial truck undertakings including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, regulation respecting audit, inspection, entry on premises and the provision of information, in at least 7 provinces.
(2) This section and sections 3 and 9, shall come into force on January 1, 1988 or on an earlier date as may be fixed by proclamation."
He said: Madam Speaker, very briefly, in order to meet our timetable, I want to say that this motion is before us because the Canadian Trucking Association indicated to all the members of the committee who studied Bill C-19 that the reverse onus test is equivalent to full deregulation as it is, for all intents and purposes, meaningless as an entry test. Therefore acceptance of Bill C-19 as it is with extended reverse onus for a five-year period means-and I hope the Government and all Members of the House will realize this-a move to full deregulation immediately.
Notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) indicated that he and the Government will do their utmost to ensure that safety on the road will be paramount and that they have been dealing with the provinces to reach an agreement to have a national safety code in place, we have now been made aware of a letter sent to the Editor of The Toronto Star by the Minister of Transport which states that most of the components of the national safety code will be in place by 1990. I think my colleagues will remember that the Minister of Transport appeared before the committee and said that it would be ready and in place for 1988.
In other words, the Minister of Transport came before the committee and made us believe that it would be ready in 1988. Some of the Conservative mepibers of the committee were ready to vote with us, the members of the Opposition, in order
to ensure that a national safety code would be implemented before we move into total deregulation. On the words of the Minister these Conservative members turned down our amendment. We have now been made aware of a letter from the Minister of Transport to The Toronto Star which states that not only will it not be ready for 1988 but some of the components of it will not even be in place by 1990.
At this very moment we know that some provinces have not yet signed the so-called unanimous agreement about which the Minister was talking. The bottom line is this. Should we accept enactment of this Bill as it is, we will be accepting full deregulation without a national safety code in place. This is why I have moved my amendment. It is to ensure that the Government will not play with the safety and security of people on the road. Thus I hope this amendment will be accepted.

Madam Speaker, there are members from all three Parties on the committee who feel some chagrin and somewhat misled, or at least led astray, as a result of the statements made by the Government with respect to the implementation of a national safety code by January 1, 1988. An amendment which we moved in committee to put the date ahead to January 1, 1989 was pooh-poohed. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), has just said, and as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), the Parliamentary Secretary and the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane) know, we questioned the Minister carefully on this matter. It has all turned out to be a pile of you-know-what, Madam Speaker.
In accordance with the requests of the Canadian Trucking Association and in light of the fact that several provinces have not yet even got around to arriving at a consensus for a national trucking code having to do with licensing, permits and safety, the amendment of the Hon. Member is perfectly reasonable. It does nothing more than require-and I guess this is the old stage of the Constitution-at least seven provinces out of ten to agree, and then there are the two Territories which have been snubbed totally throughout all of this. The committee could not even travel up there. The committee would not let us go to Yellowknife or Whitehorse. The people of the Territories have been snubbed again with respect to the Constitution. All we are asking is that until seven provinces have their regulations and their boards, by agreement with the federal Government, in place this Bill will not take effect. We tried that in committee. We were assured that everything would be ready by January 1, 1988. We will be lucky if it is ready by January 1, 1990.
The Government should try to quit kidding itself, as well as the rest of us, because it is not fooling anyone with respect to this issue. If it was smart it would take this Bill and just not deal with it anymore. It would not call third reading tomorrow. It would leave it sit until next year when we could finish dealing with it. You will be surprised to hear this, Madam Speaker, but we will not be ready to finalize it because the provinces are still horsing around on it. You can bet on that,
June 16, 1987

Madam Speaker, and I am not a betting man, especially when I think I might lose.
This amendment would impose a partial safeguard for what the Government told us repeatedly would be in place by next January 1. Everyone in this Elouse knows that it will not be ready by January 1. The implementation of this legislation has to be delayed at least one year, if we are lucky. I hope that the Government will support this motion.
